    21  Administrative Leave for Workforce Realignment and Other Purposes
    22  
    23  AGENCY: Office of Personnel Management.
    24  
    25  ACTION: Final rule.
    26  
    27  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    28  
    29  SUMMARY: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final 
    30  rule to amend its regulations governing administrative leave for 
    31  workforce realignment and other purposes. This final rule more fully 
    32  addresses the appropriate uses of administrative leave, including use 
    33  in connection with deferred resignation programs and other workforce 
    34  realignment initiatives, and for other purposes. The final rule also 
    35  clarifies when an agency may provide administrative leave during a 
    36  reduction-in-force notice period and accept or deny an employee's 
    37  request to withdraw a resignation in the context of a deferred 
    38  resignation program.
    39  
    40  DATES: This rule is effective November 18, 2026.
    41  
    42  FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Bryce Baker by telephone at (202) 606-
    43  2858 or by email at [email protected].
    44  
    45  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: OPM is issuing a final rule to amend its 
    46  regulations on administrative leave in 5 CFR part 630, subpart N, and 
    47  related regulations on reductions in force in 5 CFR 351.806 and on 
    48  resignations in 5 CFR 715.202. OPM issued a proposed rule on June 29, 
    49  2026 (91 FR 39032).
    50  
    51  I. Digest of Public Comments
    52  
    53      In response to the proposed rule, OPM received 30 comments during 
    54  the 30-day public comment period from multiple individuals, one agency 
    55  (0027), two unions (0022 and 0030), and three employee advocacy groups 
    56  (0025, 0026, and 0029). All comments were posted and made available to 
    57  the public in the docket at https://www.regulations.gov/docket/OPM-2026-0397. A reference to a comment provides the location of the item 
    58  in the public record (i.e., comments filed in response to the proposed 
    59  rule are available at https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OPM-2026-0397-nnnn where ``nnnn'' is the comment number).
    60      At the conclusion of the public comment period, OPM reviewed and 
    61  analyzed the comments. In general, the comments on the proposed 
    62  regulation changes were mixed. The comments are summarized below, 
    63  including suggestions for revisions that OPM considered and either 
    64  adopted, adopted in part, or declined to adopt, along with OPM's 
    65  supporting rationale. Section II of this preamble provides background 
    66  information. Section III responds to the comments. Section IV provides 
    67  a section-by-section analysis of the regulatory changes, section V sets 
    68  forth the regulatory analysis, and section VI addresses regulatory 
    69  compliance requirements.
    70  
    71  II. Background
    72  
    73      On December 17, 2024, OPM issued final regulations on 
    74  administrative leave that added a new subpart N in 5 CFR part 630 (89 
    75  FR 102256). The regulations in subpart N govern use of administrative 
    76  leave authorized for Federal employees under 5 U.S.C. 6329a, which was 
    77  enacted as part of the Administrative Leave Act of 2016 (section 1138 
    78  of Pub. L. 114-328, December 23, 2016). OPM subsequently
    79  
    80  [[Page 65925]]
    81  
    82  identified the need to clarify certain matters in subpart N. On June 
    83  29, 2026, OPM issued a proposed rule (91 FR 39032) pursuant to its 
    84  regulatory authority at 5 U.S.C. 6329a(c). The proposed rule addressed 
    85  acceptable and unacceptable uses of administrative leave. In 
    86  particular, OPM proposed to add a list of specific examples of 
    87  acceptable uses, including use in connection with deferred resignation 
    88  programs \1\ and other workforce restructuring initiatives. These final 
    89  regulations codify existing OPM policies on administrative leave. The 
    90  primary OPM policy documents are a ``Fact Sheet: Administrative Leave'' 
    91  and an OPM memorandum to agency Chief Human Capital Officers entitled 
    92  ``Template for Agency Administrative Leave Policies'' (CPM 2025-12, 
    93  July 30, 2025) (``Agency Policy Template'').\2\
    94  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
    95  
    96      \1\ See the following OPM memoranda on the 2025 Governmentwide 
    97  deferred resignation program available at https://www.opm.gov/chcoc/published-memos/: ``Guidance on Probationary Periods, Administrative 
    98  Leave and Details'' (January 20, 2025), ``Guidance Regarding 
    99  Deferred Resignation Program'' (January 28, 2025), ``Guidance on 
   100  Collective Bargaining Obligations in Connection with Deferred 
   101  Resignation Offer'' (February 4, 2025), and ``Legality of Deferred 
   102  Resignation Program'' (February 4, 2025).
   103      \2\ The OPM ``Fact Sheet: Administrative Leave'' is found at 
   104  https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/leave-administration/fact-sheets/administrative-leave/. The OPM memorandum 
   105  ``Template for Agency Administrative Leave Policies'' (CPM 2025-12, 
   106  July 30, 2025) is available at https://www.opm.gov/chcoc/published-memos/.
   107  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   108  
   109      In addition, the proposed rule included proposed changes to related 
   110  regulations. It proposed to amend OPM's reduction-in-force (RIF) 
   111  regulations at 5 CFR 351.806 to clarify the conditions under which an 
   112  agency may provide administrative leave during a RIF notice period. It 
   113  also proposed to amend OPM's resignation regulations at 5 CFR 715.202 
   114  to (1) provide that an agency has sole and exclusive discretion in 
   115  deciding whether to accept or deny an employee's request to withdraw a 
   116  resignation before the resignation has become effective and (2) 
   117  specifically address that an employee's receipt of benefits provided 
   118  under a deferred resignation agreement, such as paid administrative 
   119  leave, is a valid reason to deny an employee's request to withdraw a 
   120  resignation.
   121  
   122  III. Responses to Comments
   123  
   124  A. Use of Administrative Leave in Connection With a Deferred 
   125  Resignation Program
   126  
   127      A number of comments, including 0004, 0006, 0016, 0019, 0025, 0026, 
   128  and 0029, opposed codifying use of administrative leave in connection 
   129  with deferred resignation programs (DRP) as an acceptable use, arguing 
   130  that use of administrative leave for workforce restructuring 
   131  circumvents RIF procedures in 5 CFR part 351, which includes legal 
   132  safeguards to ensure that, when necessary, employees are released from 
   133  employment in an orderly manner. Commenters argued that voluntary early 
   134  retirement authority (VERA) and voluntary separation incentive payments 
   135  (VSIP) already provide bounded, accountable mechanisms with statutory 
   136  caps, and that open-ended administrative leave is designed to escape 
   137  those limits. Comment 0004 stated that OPM should reject any regulatory 
   138  framework that treats administrative leave as a preferred alternative 
   139  to lawful RIF procedures. Comment 0006 objected that administrative 
   140  leave, traditionally a short-duration tool, is being expanded into a 
   141  workforce reduction mechanism that departs from established civil 
   142  service procedures.
   143      Comment 0025 argued that deferred resignation programs require a 
   144  statutory foundation separate from section 6329a, noting that Congress 
   145  has separately authorized the VSIP and VERA programs and asserting that 
   146  section 6329a cannot be used to ``create and fund a massive 
   147  governmentwide paid separation benefit.'' The commenter cited public 
   148  reporting estimating the cost of 2025 deferred resignation programs at 
   149  approximately $11.1 billion and urged OPM to work with Congress on a 
   150  legislated transition or severance program. The commenter urged OPM to 
   151  withdraw the proposal in its entirety, begin using administrative leave 
   152  as intended by Congress, and seek legislation for any broader paid 
   153  transition or severance program.
   154      Comment 0016 similarly argued that VERA and VSIP already provide 
   155  bounded, accountable voluntary-reduction tools with statutory caps, 
   156  making open-ended administrative leave unnecessary, and that codifying 
   157  open-ended administrative leave as a ``transition-to-separation tool'' 
   158  invites agencies to route around the disciplined mechanisms Congress 
   159  enacted, and to do so with public funds and no meaningful oversight. 
   160  Comment 0026 recommended that OPM work with Congress to raise the 
   161  statutory cap on voluntary separation incentive payments to make it a 
   162  more useful tool. An individual commenter argued that the proposed rule 
   163  weakens the due process protections that have sustained a competent, 
   164  professional, merit-based civil service, and that it will harm Federal 
   165  recruitment and retention and requested withdrawal of the proposed 
   166  rule. Due process concerns are addressed further in section III.F.
   167      OPM disagrees that a separate statutory authorization is required 
   168  to use administrative leave in conjunction with a DRP. Administrative 
   169  leave provided in connection with a DRP is administrative leave under 
   170  section 6329a, provided pursuant to a written agreement in which the 
   171  employee voluntarily commits to separate on a specified future date. 
   172  Such leave is not ``placed'' on an unwilling employee; it is a benefit 
   173  the employee elects to accept as part of a voluntary transition to 
   174  separation. The concerns that animated the Administrative Leave Act--
   175  open-ended, involuntary removal of employees from the workplace during 
   176  unresolved personnel matters--are not implicated where an employee has 
   177  voluntarily agreed to separate and to the terms of the transition 
   178  period.
   179      The existence of VSIP and VERA does not preclude the use of 
   180  administrative leave as a complementary workforce-shaping tool. Those 
   181  authorities address different benefits--lump-sum incentive payments and 
   182  modified retirement eligibility, respectively--and nothing in those 
   183  statutes states or implies that they are the exclusive means by which 
   184  agencies may facilitate voluntary separations. Indeed, the new Sec.  
   185  630.1403(c)(9) expressly contemplates that administrative leave may be 
   186  used in conjunction with VSIP and VERA. Section 630.1403(c)(9) is 
   187  limited to cases where employees sign voluntary written agreements to 
   188  separate on a specified future date and receive administrative leave as 
   189  a part of that voluntary agreement. Agencies have long had discretion 
   190  to determine how employees in a transition-to-separation posture will 
   191  be utilized, and the final rule confirms that discretion while 
   192  subjecting it to Governmentwide limits established by OPM and 
   193  applicable agency limits.
   194      OPM acknowledges that VERA and VSIP are separate authorities with 
   195  their own limits; the inclusion of those authorities in the same 
   196  example is descriptive of the range of voluntary transition tools and 
   197  does not subject administrative leave to, or exempt it from, the 
   198  statutory conditions governing VERA or VSIP, which continue to apply on 
   199  their own terms.
   200      OPM does not agree that this final rule expands administrative 
   201  leave into a workforce reduction tool that circumvents RIF procedures. 
   202  The final rule does not waive, suspend, or displace any requirement of 
   203  5 CFR part 351. Retention registers, retention standing, veterans' 
   204  preference, and all
   205  
   206  [[Page 65926]]
   207  
   208  other RIF requirements continue to apply in full to any involuntary RIF 
   209  separation. The only change made to part 351 is to Sec.  351.806, which 
   210  addresses an employee's duty status during the RIF notice period. 
   211  Paragraph (a) retains the general expectation that an employee will 
   212  remain in a duty status during the notice period. It replaces the 
   213  ``when possible'' language with ``under ordinary circumstances,'' which 
   214  is consistent with the language used in 5 CFR 752.404(b)(3) that 
   215  addresses duty status during an advanced notice period in connection 
   216  with a proposed removal or suspension. The new paragraph (b) permits--
   217  but does not require--administrative leave for all or part of that 
   218  period when the agency determines such leave is appropriate. This 
   219  regulatory clarification is consistent with OPM policy guidance \3\ 
   220  which already provided that an authorized agency official may provide 
   221  administrative leave between an employee's receipt of a notice of 
   222  involuntary separation and the effective date of that separation.
   223  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   224  
   225      \3\ See section D.1.b in OPM memorandum ``Template for Agency 
   226  Administrative Leave Policies'' (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025), which 
   227  is available at https://www.opm.gov/chcoc/published-memos/.
   228  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   229  
   230      New Sec.  630.1403(c)(10) and revised Sec.  351.806 address only 
   231  whether an employee may be placed in a paid, non-duty status during a 
   232  RIF notice period. Those provisions do not alter the substantive or 
   233  procedural requirements governing RIF, which continue to apply in full 
   234  whenever an agency conducts a RIF. Nothing in this rule authorizes an 
   235  agency to bypass RIF competition, retention registers, or appeal 
   236  rights.
   237      As to cost, OPM addresses costs in section III.B and regulatory-
   238  impact matters in section III.E. OPM notes here that the DRPs conducted 
   239  in 2025 were undertaken pursuant to existing regulatory authority and 
   240  OPM guidance; this rule codifies the availability of administrative 
   241  leave for DRP programs prospectively, subject to the limits described 
   242  above. OPM agrees that Congress remains free to enact additional 
   243  workforce-transition authorities but disagrees that such legislation is 
   244  a prerequisite to the uses identified in this rule. The sponsors of the 
   245  Administrative Leave Act were concerned about costs associated with 
   246  open-ended investigations of employees and did not consider a use of 
   247  administrative leave that would produce long-term cost savings by 
   248  facilitating workforce reductions.
   249      OPM declines to withdraw the rule or to make changes based on this 
   250  line of comments. The final rule is a lawful exercise of OPM's 
   251  authority under 5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1), strengthens the regulatory 
   252  framework by converting policy guidance into binding prohibitions and 
   253  clarifying acceptable uses, preserves the duty-status presumption 
   254  during RIF notice periods, and does not alter the statutory 10-workday 
   255  limit or the investigative- and notice-leave framework of section 
   256  6329b.
   257  
   258  B. Cost of Administrative Leave and DRP
   259  
   260      Several comments, including 0004, 0016, 0022, and 0025, objected to 
   261  the cost of using administrative leave in conjunction with a DRP. 
   262  Comment 0004 stated the 2025 deferred resignation programs showed 
   263  waste, including paying employees who performed no work and later 
   264  rehiring. The commenter believes a full accounting of the DRPs should 
   265  be conducted before similar programs are codified in regulation. 
   266  Comment 0016 noted that the 2025 DRP placed tens of thousands of 
   267  employees in paid non-duty status for months while delivering no work 
   268  to the public, a direct payroll expenditure for zero output, compounded 
   269  by the loss of institutional knowledge, the collapse of continuity in 
   270  mission-critical functions, and the documented degradation of agency 
   271  capacity that followed. Comment 0022 commented that the proposed rule 
   272  attempts to justify the administration's costly workforce reduction 
   273  efforts, including widespread use of administrative leave, by promising 
   274  ``large long-term savings'' without providing concrete support or 
   275  considering downstream effects of letting employees participate in DRP.
   276      Comment 0022 also stated that OPM failed to provide concrete 
   277  support that justifies costly workforce reduction efforts, even as it 
   278  acknowledges the costs of the workforce reduction initiatives that 
   279  began in early 2025. The organization cited two recent studies that 
   280  highlight significant expenses tied to these workforce reduction 
   281  programs: (1) a June 2026 study estimated that deferred resignation 
   282  programs alone have cost at least $11 billion; and (2) another analysis 
   283  from April 2026 found that the Government paid approximately $4.5 
   284  billion in salary and benefits to employees who were not working under 
   285  DRP agreements.
   286      OPM respectfully disagrees with the commenters on the costs 
   287  associated with the original DRP. OPM acknowledged in the proposed rule 
   288  that there is a temporary cost to providing administrative leave and 
   289  stated its judgment that use of administrative leave in connection with 
   290  deferred resignation programs and other workforce restructuring 
   291  initiatives can generate long-term savings by reducing Federal staffing 
   292  levels. OPM did not project costs or savings from the proposed 
   293  regulations themselves because the regulations codify Governmentwide 
   294  policies already in place, and OPM does not expect codification to 
   295  produce significant changes in the usage of administrative leave.
   296      Further, OPM policy guidance has stated that use of administrative 
   297  leave in connection with DRP is in the interest of the agency and of 
   298  the Government as a whole because it facilitates workforce 
   299  restructuring and realignment efforts leading to a leaner, less 
   300  expensive, less wasteful, more efficient, and more mission-focused 
   301  Federal workforce. OPM also notes that this policy is not open-ended: 
   302  beginning in calendar year 2026, use of administrative leave by an 
   303  employee in connection with a workforce realignment initiative is 
   304  limited to 12 weeks in any individual instance unless a higher 
   305  threshold has been jointly approved by OPM and the Office of Management 
   306  and Budget. In addition, Sec.  630.1403(a)(6) requires an authorized 
   307  agency official to consider the effect on productivity and mission 
   308  needs and the strength of the justification for using appropriated 
   309  funds.
   310      OPM calculates that DRP separations in 2025 represented a workforce 
   311  reduction of over 6 percent, which contributed to the overall reduction 
   312  of the Federal workforce of over 12 percent from December 2024 to March 
   313  2026. Those workforce reductions create significant long-term savings 
   314  even after accounting for the one-time costs of DRP administrative 
   315  leave, which represent less than 3 percent of total basic payroll for 
   316  Federal employees. Because the payroll savings from a smaller workforce 
   317  recur in every subsequent fiscal year while the administrative leave 
   318  outlays are one-time transition costs, the long-term savings 
   319  substantially exceed the short-term costs even under the commenters' 
   320  own estimates.
   321      OPM makes no changes in the regulations in response to this line of 
   322  comments.
   323  
   324  C. 10-Workday Limit
   325  
   326      Comment 0025 asserted that the proposed rule exceeds OPM's 
   327  authority under the Administrative Leave Act of 2016, 5 U.S.C. 6329a-
   328  6329c, by establishing a regulatory exception to the statutory 10-
   329  workday calendar year limit. The commenter argued that the section 
   330  6329a(b) 10-workday calendar-
   331  
   332  [[Page 65927]]
   333  
   334  year limit reflects Congress's intent to curb extended agency-directed 
   335  paid non-duty status, that OPM's authority under section 6329a(c)(1) to 
   336  prescribe acceptable uses does not include authority to override that 
   337  limit, and that authorizing months of administrative leave for 
   338  workforce realignment, RIF notice periods, and settlements would render 
   339  the statutory cap ``optional and meaningless.'' The commenter urged OPM 
   340  to withdraw the proposal and seek legislation for any broader paid 
   341  transition or severance program. Similarly, comment 0029 asserted that 
   342  the proposed rule conflicts with the 10-workday limit Congress enacted 
   343  in section 6329a(b)(1) by ``re-authorizing exactly the indefinite, 
   344  uncontestable leave status Congress acted to eliminate.''
   345      However, comment 0029 supported retaining the language found in 
   346  proposed Sec.  630.1403(b)(3) concerning the use of administrative 
   347  leave for investigative purposes. A labor organization (0030) similarly 
   348  argued that the text and structure of the Act--including the separately 
   349  defined and expressly limited investigative leave authority in 5 U.S.C. 
   350  6329b--show that Congress withheld the power to provide unlimited 
   351  amounts of administrative leave, and cited the sense-of-Congress 
   352  findings accompanying the Act (5 U.S.C. 6329a note) that agency use of 
   353  administrative leave had exceeded reasonable amounts and that 
   354  administrative leave should be used sparingly.
   355      OPM disagrees that the rule exceeds its statutory authority. 
   356  Congress expressly directed OPM to ``prescribe regulations to carry 
   357  out'' section 6329a, including regulations governing the ``acceptable 
   358  agency uses of administrative leave'' and the recording of such leave 
   359  (5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1)). The final rule is an exercise of precisely that 
   360  delegated authority: it identifies acceptable and prohibited uses of 
   361  administrative leave and codifies existing Governmentwide policies to 
   362  promote consistency and accountability across agencies.
   363      The final rule does not waive, extend, or otherwise modify the 10-
   364  workday limit in section 6329a(b)(1). As OPM explained in the December 
   365  2024 final rule (89 FR 102256), the statutory limit applies where an 
   366  agency ``place[s]'' an employee on administrative leave for 
   367  investigative purposes. The 10-workday limit directly connects to a 
   368  provision in the investigative leave law (section 6329b(b)(3)(A)), 
   369  which bars placing an employee on investigative leave until the 10-
   370  workday limit is reached.
   371      The final rule preserves and indeed strengthens the statutory 
   372  framework. New Sec.  630.1403(b)(3) provides clarity by expressly 
   373  prohibiting use of administrative leave for investigative purposes once 
   374  the employee has reached the 10-workday limit. If necessary, an agency 
   375  may then use investigative leave under section 6329b, with all of that 
   376  section's procedural safeguards, approvals, time limits, and reporting 
   377  requirements. Thus, the final rule gives fuller effect to the statutory 
   378  scheme Congress designed for the specific problem that motivated the 
   379  Administrative Leave Act--prolonged, agency-directed removal of 
   380  employees from the workplace during personnel investigations.
   381      The commenter's reading--under which the 10-workday limit would 
   382  govern all extended uses of administrative leave--is inconsistent with 
   383  the position the commenter itself acknowledges: that general 
   384  administrative leave for purposes such as voting, blood donation, and 
   385  emergency closures remains outside the cap. The statute does not 
   386  enumerate acceptable purposes; it delegates that task to OPM. Nothing 
   387  in the text of section 6329a confines OPM's authority under subsection 
   388  (c)(1) to brief or de minimis uses, and the enumerated examples in 
   389  Sec.  630.1403(c) operate within, not around, the statutory limits: 
   390  uses that fall within the investigative context remain subject to the 
   391  10-workday limit, which when reached triggers coverage under section 
   392  6329b, while the workforce-realignment uses in paragraphs (c)(9) 
   393  through (c)(11) address categorically different circumstances, 
   394  discussed further below. The December 17, 2024, final rule cited by the 
   395  commenter included this sentence: ``An incidence of administrative 
   396  leave lasting more than 1 workday may be approved when determined to be 
   397  appropriate by an agency'' (5 CFR 630.1403(a)(3)). This final rule 
   398  simply adds specific examples of appropriate uses of administrative 
   399  leave for periods of more than 1 workday.

summary.text:
**Locating amendment language**

I’m narrowing the focus to the closing portion of the document, where the actual amendment language should appear. I need to identify the precise lines rather than relying on surrounding discussion, so I’m checking the ending carefully and separating the proposed changes from commentary or procedural notes. Once I find that wording, I can present it accurately and avoid mixing in unrelated material.

[2026-21320: lines 1080-1239 of 2132, FR page 65933]
  1080  submissions from labor organizations and public-interest groups, 
  1081  indicating that interested parties had an adequate opportunity to 
  1082  comment. Moreover, because the rule largely codifies Governmentwide 
  1083  policies that have been publicly available since July 2025, interested 
  1084  parties were already familiar with the substance of the proposals. OPM 
  1085  declines to reopen or extend the comment period.
  1086  
  1087  M. Duty Status Presumption During RIF Notice Periods (Sec.  351.806)
  1088  
  1089      Comment 0025 urged OPM to preserve the existing duty-status 
  1090  presumption during RIF notice periods, arguing that RIF notices are not 
  1091  disciplinary, that employees perform valuable transition work during 
  1092  notice periods, that existing authorities already address unusual 
  1093  cases, and that OPM has not identified a gap warranting a RIF-specific 
  1094  administrative-leave authorization.
  1095      The final rule preserves the duty-status presumption with a minor 
  1096  change in terminology. Revised Sec.  351.806(a) provides that ``[u]nder 
  1097  ordinary circumstances, an employee will remain in a duty status during 
  1098  the notice period.'' The change from ``when possible'' to ``under 
  1099  ordinary circumstances'' conforms the RIF regulation to the parallel 
  1100  standard in 5 CFR 752.404(b)(3) governing notice periods for proposed 
  1101  removals and suspensions, and more accurately reflects that the 
  1102  determination involves an assessment of circumstances rather than 
  1103  literal possibility. Paragraph (b) then confirms--consistent with the 
  1104  Agency Policy Template--that an agency may place a RIF-affected 
  1105  employee on administrative leave for all or part of the notice period 
  1106  when the agency determines that such leave is appropriate and 
  1107  consistent with part 630, subpart N.
  1108      OPM agrees that RIF notice periods are not inherently disciplinary 
  1109  and that employees frequently perform valuable work during them; that 
  1110  is why duty status remains the default. But circumstances vary: an 
  1111  agency may determine, for example, that continued systems access during 
  1112  a large-scale reorganization presents security or records-integrity 
  1113  risks, that available work has genuinely ceased for the affected 
  1114  positions, or that other Government interests warrant non-duty status. 
  1115  The rule leaves that judgment to the agency familiar with the facts, 
  1116  rather than requiring agencies to rely on a patchwork of assignment, 
  1117  telework, and leave authorities that may not fit the circumstances of a 
  1118  RIF. Nothing in the revision permits use of administrative leave 
  1119  inconsistent with subpart N of part 630.
  1120  
  1121  N. Nomenclature Change (``Grant'' To ``Provide'') (Part 630, Subpart N)
  1122  
  1123      Comment 0025 objected to replacing ``grant/granted/granting'' with 
  1124  ``provide/provided/providing'' throughout subpart N, arguing that the 
  1125  change extends agency-directed administrative leave beyond the limits 
  1126  of the Act and the 2024 rule by encompassing leave imposed without 
  1127  employee consent.
  1128      OPM disagrees that the nomenclature change effects any substantive 
  1129  expansion of authority. As explained in the proposed rule, ``grant'' 
  1130  inaccurately implies that administrative leave is furnished only at an 
  1131  employee's request, which has never been the case--for example, 
  1132  employees have long been placed on administrative leave for 
  1133  investigative purposes without their consent, a practice Congress 
  1134  itself recognized and regulated in sections 6329a and 6329b. 
  1135  ``Provide'' is a neutral term that accurately describes the provision 
  1136  of administrative leave with or without the employee's consent. The 
  1137  statutory 10-workday limit continues to apply to employees ``placed'' 
  1138  on administrative leave for investigative purposes, as provided in 
  1139  Sec.  630.1404(a). For other uses of administrative leave, which may be 
  1140  voluntarily accepted or imposed without the employee's consent, we are 
  1141  using the term ``provide.'' The terminology change harmonizes the 
  1142  regulatory text with existing practice and with the structure of the 
  1143  statute; it does not authorize any use of administrative leave that 
  1144  would otherwise be impermissible.
  1145  
  1146  O. Prohibition on Administrative Leave for Poll Workers (Sec.  
  1147  630.1403(b)(5))
  1148  
  1149      Several comments, including 0016, 0022, 0030, and 0031, objected to 
  1150  the prohibition of administrative leave for service as a poll worker or 
  1151  poll observer found in proposed Sec.  630.1403(b)(5). The commenters 
  1152  argued that the prohibition is unrelated to workforce realignment, 
  1153  discourages civic participation amid documented poll-worker shortages, 
  1154  saves little, and reverses OPM's prior guidance that agencies allow up 
  1155  to 4 hours of administrative leave for nonpartisan poll service. A 
  1156  labor organization (comment 0022) characterized limited administrative 
  1157  leave for nonpartisan poll service as an important, pro-democracy 
  1158  policy choice. Another labor organization (comment 0030) argued that 
  1159  OPM offered no reasoned explanation or evidence for the prohibition and 
  1160  characterized it as an attempt to stifle Federal employees' exercise of 
  1161  their constitutional rights.
  1162      OPM notes that the changes in the administrative leave regulations 
  1163  are not limited to changes related to workforce realignment. OPM 
  1164  acknowledges that this provision changes OPM's prior policies that 
  1165  agencies could allow limited administrative leave for nonpartisan poll 
  1166  service. However, those prior policies were a departure from 
  1167  longstanding Governmentwide policies that existed before 2020, which 
  1168  focused on administrative leave for voting, not for poll workers. Based 
  1169  on its authority to regulate acceptable uses of administrative leave, 
  1170  OPM has determined that administrative leave should be limited to the 
  1171  purpose of ensuring employees a reasonable opportunity to vote (see 
  1172  Sec.  630.1403(c)(2)). OPM policy (section E.1.d of the Agency Policy 
  1173  Template) already provided that administrative leave may not be used to 
  1174  cover service by poll workers or poll observers in connection with 
  1175  elections, whether that service is partisan or nonpartisan and whether 
  1176  paid or unpaid. Limiting administrative leave to voting itself also 
  1177  avoids placing agencies in the position
  1178  
  1179  [[Page 65934]]
  1180  
  1181  of assessing whether particular election-related service is partisan or 
  1182  nonpartisan.
  1183      The prohibition does not restrict any employee's ability to serve 
  1184  as a poll worker or poll observer; it addresses only whether that 
  1185  service will be subsidized with paid leave from Federal duty, and a 
  1186  decision not to subsidize an activity does not infringe the right to 
  1187  engage in it (see Regan v. Taxation With Representation of Washington, 
  1188  461 U.S. 540, 549 (1983)). Employees who wish to serve as poll workers 
  1189  or poll observers may use other available workforce flexibilities, 
  1190  including annual leave, compensatory time off earned via overtime work, 
  1191  compensatory time off for travel, credit hours under a flexible work 
  1192  schedule, an adjustment of working hours under a flexible work 
  1193  schedule, or leave without pay. OPM makes no change in response to 
  1194  these comments.
  1195  
  1196  P. Administrative Leave Prior to a Holiday (Sec.  630.1403(c)(5))
  1197  
  1198      Regarding Sec.  630.1403(c)(5), comment 0024 stated that early 
  1199  dismissal before a Federal holiday should not be subject to a hard 2-
  1200  hour cap and that longer dismissals should be available for particular 
  1201  occasions, including days of national observance.
  1202      OPM notes that Sec.  630.1403(c)(5) does not establish a hard cap 
  1203  since it states that the administrative leave should ``generally'' be 
  1204  no more than 2 hours. This regulation should be read with sections 
  1205  D.2.d and E.2.a of the Agency Policy Template (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 
  1206  2025), which provide that such leave may not exceed 2 hours unless 
  1207  specifically approved by the agency head. The flexibility the commenter 
  1208  seeks for longer periods of dismissal for particular occasions is 
  1209  therefore already available through agency head approval. 
  1210  Presidentially directed closures and days of national observance 
  1211  provided by the President using his or her constitutional authority as 
  1212  head of the Executive branch are not administrative leave under 5 
  1213  U.S.C. 6329a and are not governed by subpart N or by an agency's 
  1214  administrative leave policy (Agency Policy Template, section A.2.b and 
  1215  Appendix 1). Such occasions are therefore outside this rulemaking. OPM 
  1216  notes separately that proposed Sec.  630.1403(b)(1) continues to 
  1217  prohibit use of administrative leave to mark the memory of a deceased 
  1218  former Federal official (see also 5 U.S.C. 6105).
  1219

summary.text:
**Clarifying duty status**

I’m distinguishing between the rule currently in effect and language adopted for a later effective date. Based on the available proposal discussion, the current version of 5 CFR 351.806 says that, when possible, an employee remains in duty status throughout the notice period. I’m avoiding claims about additional exceptions because the complete current text isn’t available here. For the future version, I would identify the adopted wording separately and clearly note that it is not yet operative on November 14.**Evaluating leave authority**

I’m separating the rules applicable on November 14 from provisions adopted for future use. The described framework allows annual leave with or without consent, leave without pay with consent, and nonpay status without consent when work or funding is unavailable. Administrative leave appears to depend on the applicable policy or companion leave provision. I’m not yet certain about its consent requirement or any duration cap, so I should verify the precise adopted text before stating whether the leave is unlimited or subject to a defined maximum.

summary.text:
**Determining leave limits**

I’m reading the adopted text as imposing no separate maximum duration on this administrative leave. Under the relevant provision, leave may continue from the employee’s receipt of the reduction-in-force notice until the effective separation date. The broader governmentwide limits appear to apply to other administrative-leave categories, not this notice-period provision. I should distinguish that from separate 12-week workforce-realignment limits, which do not govern this situation. Prior guidance also recognized agency-authorized administrative leave during this interval.**Checking compliance steps**

I’m assessing each item against the applicable reduction-in-force rules. The competitive area appears properly described and organizationally based, but its designation occurred within the required 90-day window and lacked advance approval, creating a compliance defect. One employee remains excluded because she is serving an initial probationary period. Another employee, however, is serving supervisory probation rather than initial probation, so she should compete and appear on the retention register. Finally, I’m calculating the relevant cutoff as September 13 for notices issued October 13.

**Applying rating rules**

I’m excluding the October 2 rating because it was entered after the cutoff, which falls on September 13. For the five usable ratings, the two Level 5 scores are 7, and the two Level 4 scores are 5; the missing proxy is therefore 6. That produces a performance score of 18, not 15, because I’m using the average of the actual values rather than assuming Level 3.

I’m also rejecting the proposed two-point addition: it cannot be applied automatically to every quality-step-increase employee.**Applying additional rules**

I’m treating the advance announcement as insufficient by itself. Additional points are restricted to the qualifying rating pattern and eligible employees; a five-level pattern does not fit the stated single-pattern limitation, and applying points regardless of rating is improper.

For the tie, identical performance, veterans’ preference, and tenure factors allow the agency to select any tied employee.

I’m also finding the proposed release improper because retaining an employee on a specifically limited temporary promotion through March 2027 while releasing a competing employee conflicts with the applicable retention-order rule.

**Applying assessment rules**

I’m distinguishing between the employee’s competitive level and the assessment requirement. Silva appears eligible for an exception because, during the relevant five-year period ending October 13, 2026, Silva held the same position and had received a Level 4 rating in 2022. Assuming the position was substantially identical, no new qualification assessment was required.

The online questionnaire is different: an assessment cannot rely solely or principally on an automatically scored self-rating. It must let employees demonstrate relevant qualifications and be grounded in job analysis.**Evaluating retention periods**

I’m separating the initial 60-day retention from the additional 60-day extension. The first period may be permissible if the agency establishes that the employee’s duties cannot be assumed within 90 days without undue interruption and provides the required notice. Merely citing project completion may not establish those facts.

The second extension appears problematic because exceptions generally stand alone and cannot be sequenced or stacked. I’m checking whether that bar reaches the continuing-duty exception as well; at minimum, the agency likely must select one applicable exception, using only the longest permitted period.

**Interpreting exception limits**

I’m examining whether the anti-stacking language in §351.608(a)(3) applies only among temporary exceptions listed within §351.608, or whether it also prevents combining a continuing exception under §351.607 with a temporary exception under §351.608. The wording “under a paragraph in this section” appears limited to §351.608 itself. That suggests an agency may first use the §351.607 exception and then apply a §351.608 temporary exception, unless the preamble or broader policy indicates otherwise. I’m checking that distinction carefully.**Clarifying exception stacking**

I’m focusing on whether “another exception” refers only to the other exceptions listed within §351.608, or whether it broadly prohibits sequential extensions involving §351.607 as well. The question may deliberately test that distinction by describing an initial 60-day extension under a continuing exception, followed by another 60 days under a general temporary exception. I’m also checking whether the rule limits any further extension altogether, rather than merely preventing simultaneous or sequential use of multiple temporary exceptions. The preamble’s discussion of “stacking” should help resolve that ambiguity.

summary.text:
**Interpreting exception structure**

I’m examining whether the cited provision prohibits combining exceptions from separate sections or only prevents stacking exceptions within §351.608 itself. The wording appears limited: each exception under a paragraph in that section must stand alone and cannot be sequenced with another exception. Because §351.607 is a separate section, its continuing or temporary exception might not fall within that restriction. I’m checking the surrounding regulatory language and preamble to determine whether the broader framework treats these exceptions as combinable or still mutually exclusive.

summary.text:
**Interpreting exception sequencing**

I’m weighing whether exceptions under different provisions can be stacked. The restriction appears to apply only to exceptions “under a paragraph in this section,” which may leave room for combining an exception under §351.607 with one under §351.608. Still, that reading could be challenged because using a temporary exception after a continuing exception may amount to prohibited sequencing. I need to distinguish the provisions’ timing and purposes: one concerns continuing exceptions, while temporary exceptions apply after a reduction-in-force effective date.**Assessing cumulative exceptions**

I’m reading §351.607 as permitting an extended separation date when duties cannot be transferred within the specified period. A temporary exception under §351.608 applies after the reduction-in-force becomes effective. The wording of §351.608(a)(3) specifically addresses exceptions “under a paragraph in this section,” creating a textual argument that §351.607 is outside its express prohibition. Still, because the arrangement could be viewed as stacking exceptions to retain the same employee, the safer conclusion is that cumulative use is not permitted, subject to the provision’s precise wording and explanatory materials.

**Evaluating exception overlap**

I’m distinguishing between the continuing-duty provision in §351.607 and the separate exceptions in §351.608(g). Section 351.607 may permit continued service when the duties cannot be taken over within 90 days, and it does not appear to impose the same duration limit as the temporary exceptions. The text seems to prohibit stacking among §351.608 exceptions, but I’m not seeing an equally clear bar on combining §351.607 with §351.608(g). I should therefore treat the result as ambiguous rather than definitively invalid, while emphasizing any required written notices and conditions.**Interpreting stacking language**

I’m weighing two readings of §351.608(a)(3). The narrower reading limits the prohibition to exceptions listed within §351.608, meaning a §351.607 period followed by §351.608(g) might be permissible. The broader reading treats “another exception” as including §351.607, which would prohibit combining them. Because the provision begins by referring to exceptions under that section, the wording is genuinely uncertain. I should identify the combination as legally contestable rather than confidently compliant or noncompliant, while explaining both interpretations.

**Interpreting exception periods**

I’m examining whether the rule allows an agency to apply more than one exception, including exceptions 607 and 608, and then select the one providing the longest period. The continuing exception under 607 may not be temporary and may lack a defined maximum, while the wording could refer only to exceptions under 351.608.

I’m also checking corrections to the CTAP definition in 5 CFR 330.602. A revision may have unintentionally removed subparagraphs (A) and (B), with a later correction restoring them. I need to verify the exact text in the published rule and correction.

summary.text:
**Comparing regulatory text**

I’m noticing that Q10(a) appears incomplete: it introduces a competitive-service group at GS-15 or below but provides no circumstances explaining when someone is displaced. The missing subparagraphs likely resulted from an inadvertent omission, which the correction addresses. Under §351, subpart G, declining an offer with a lower representative rate still permits displacement; declining an offer with at least the current rate does not, provided it involves the same schedule and full-time status.

Q11 requires comparing the proposed and final texts comprehensively because the amendments contain substantive differences.**Comparing amendment sections**

I’m identifying the affected parts—316, 330, 351, 353, 359, 362, and 430—and comparing their proposed wording with the final text. Because this may involve several hundred lines, I’m planning to review the corresponding sections sequentially and distinguish substantive changes from formatting or editorial edits. I’ll first examine the proposal’s regulatory text, then compare each section against its final counterpart and record every meaningful difference rather than assuming the proposal and final rule are identical.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

summary.text:
**Comparing regulatory amendments**

I’m comparing both regulatory texts line by line because the request asks for every substantive difference between the proposals. I’ve already identified one apparent change involving student appointment tenure: one version refers to a “competitive service tenure group” after the initial probationary period, while the other appears to modify that language. I’m continuing through the relevant sections to verify the wording and distinguish genuine changes from formatting or editorial differences.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

summary.text:
**Comparing regulatory text**

I’m narrowing the comparison to substantive amendments in the regulatory text, rather than preambles or merely stylistic changes. Citation formatting, punctuation, capitalization, and page references generally shouldn’t count, though changes to statutory authority may matter if they alter the legal substance.

For Part 330, I’m noting that the proposal’s instruction ending paragraph 4 with “and” was removed. The final version instead revises paragraph 5 and adds paragraph 6. I’m continuing to compare the complete regulatory text for similarly substantive differences.**Identifying substantive changes**

I’m distinguishing wording changes that affect meaning from simple grammatical improvements. The revised automated-assessment language narrows and clarifies the requirement, so I’m treating it as a real difference.

For the CTAP definition, the final amendatory instruction appears to replace the entire first paragraph, unintentionally omitting subparagraphs (i) and (ii); a later correction restored them. I’m recording both the originally published omission and the correction separately.

I’m also noting that ICTAP and related provisions replace “probationary or trial period” with “probationary period” and cite §11.2, removing the broader trial-period reference.

**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m comparing the proposal with the final text of §351.202(d). The final version reframes the rule from broadly excluding employees from the part to identifying employees who are excluded from reduction-in-force competition, then adds consequences and notice provisions in paragraphs (3) and (4).

The appointment categories also change. The proposal covered temporary or term appointments of one year or less under subparts C or D; the final text limits that category to temporary appointments of one year or less under subpart D, removing term appointments from it.

For trial periods, the proposal used an agency-issued specific-notice date, while the final text simply refers to an employee serving a trial period.**Comparing definitions**

I’m identifying several substantive changes between the proposal and final text. The final rule removes the express “as-of” date and adds provisions addressing the agency’s ability to retain or release employees, along with a separate notice paragraph.

In §351.203, the furlough definition changes from a duration dependent specifically on congressional action to one where the ultimate duration is simply unknown to the agency at the outset. The probationary-period cross-reference changes from “this chapter” to “this part.” The rating-of-record definition also changes its citation from §430.208(d) to §430.208(e), while revising language about performance assessment and adding a reference to summary levels.

**Comparing regulatory changes**

I’m comparing the proposed and final wording section by section, separating substantive changes from editorial ones. The final rule adds language defining a restoration-protected employee and appears to address USERRA or military-service considerations, so I’m noting that as a potentially meaningful addition.

I’m also flagging §351.204, where the final text adds responsibility for ensuring reductions in force comply with applicable laws and merit-system principles. By contrast, the §351.301 change may be mostly editorial: the final version simplifies how it removes a parenthetical phrase without clearly changing the outcome.**Assessing final revisions**

I’m treating the §351.301 wording as non-substantive because the final rule appears to remove the same phrase despite using a different description.

The §351.302 revisions matter more: the final text expands beyond one referenced procedure to include other procedures required by law, regulation, or appointment terms. It also clarifies that agencies must determine each employee’s preference and provide information individually, which could have operational significance.

The §351.402 change is substantive, adding approval and public-availability requirements. Finally, §351.502 changes key timing events from notice issuance to employee receipt, affecting several employee categories.

**Comparing regulatory revisions**

I’m distinguishing substantive changes from simple drafting corrections. The wording in §351.502(b)(3) appears to be only a grammatical fix, while §351.503(a)(1) makes a meaningful change by replacing “Minimally Successful” with “Minimally Satisfactory” and updating the cross-reference from §430.208(d) to §430.208(e). The §351.503(b)(3) revision also seems stylistic rather than substantive. I still need to verify the exact language in §351.503(c)(4) and §351.503(d), especially the rating conditions, exceptional criteria, and updated references.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

summary.text:
**Comparing regulatory changes**

I’m identifying substantive differences between the proposed and final texts, including provisions that appeared in the proposal but were omitted from the final rule. The proposed changes to §351.604(b) and (d) should therefore be listed, while clarifying that the final rule leaves §351.604 unchanged. Section 351.605 also changed materially: the final rule reorganizes the notice requirements into separate paragraphs (c) and (d), with more specific content, whereas the proposal incorporated the notice language within paragraph (b).**Comparing notice provisions**

I’m separating stylistic changes from substantive ones. The reference to paragraph (a) and the wording about employees excluded under §351.202(d) appear largely clarifying, while the citation formatting is non-substantive. The major change is in §351.605: the final rule creates a distinct written-notice requirement under §351.801, specifies the competitive area and mandatory content, and adds a separate paragraph explaining that ranking and retention-register procedures are unnecessary. I also need to verify whether §351.606 adds restoration protections absent from the proposal; if so, that belongs in the comparison.

summary.text:
**Comparing regulatory changes**

I’m identifying substantive and wording differences across the sections. In §351.503(d)(3), “criteria readily” versus “criteria” appears to be a minor grammatical change. Section §351.504 is more meaningful: “should be identified” becomes “must be identified,” strengthening the obligation, while the paragraph formatting changes only citation style.

I’m also noting that §351.505 corrects a cross-reference from proposed §351.503(b) to final §351.504(b), which may affect interpretation. In §351.506, the final wording clarifies employee performance and service-computation dates, adds an access-related caveat, and provides more detailed FOIA and privacy restrictions.**Assessing substantive revisions**

I’m noting that the final language narrows “no right to review” to this section, preserving rights available under other statutes or regulations. Section §351.507 appears largely unchanged, aside from a likely editorial wording correction.

Section §351.606 is substantially rewritten: it now addresses both relevant exceptions, establishes mandatory pass-over and reassignment steps, references placement procedures, lists unaffected provisions, specifies documentation, and corrects a cross-reference. Section §351.701 also receives a major restructuring, retaining the basic framework while adding more detailed provisions concerning pay rates, criteria, grade intervals, locations, and pay bands.

**Comparing revised language**

I’m comparing the proposal with the final text and finding that most provisions remain substantially unchanged. The main visible edits are the addition of a “General” heading, revised wording from “minimally successful” to “minimally satisfactory” for Level 2, and a slight restructuring of the cross-reference in paragraph (b), along with subsection headings. The proposed paragraphs (c)(1) and (c)(2), and later provisions, otherwise appear consistent. One substantive addition is in §351.702: a new subsection (v) limits assessment when the employee held the same job within five years and had a Level 3 rating.**Identifying substantive changes**

I’m noting several wording and structural differences. The automated-assessment provision changes from “does not solely include or principally rely on a self-assessment” to language stating it does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment. Section 351.705 revises paragraph (a), while §351.802 adds introductory language and updates references concerning veterans’ preferences and the relevant regulations. Part 353 adds an entirely new §353.209 on retention protections. Part 359 removes a clause concerning congressional action, paralleling the furlough-definition revision. The Pathways provisions appear unchanged.

summary.text:
**Reconciling final amendments**

I’m tracking several changes that still need to appear in the final comparison: an amendment to §351.805(b), removal of §351.604, added notice language in §351.202, mandatory subgroup treatment in §351.504, a possible retiree correction in §351.505, and revised records in §351.506.

I’m also checking the retention and assignment cascades in Q12, using the stated October 5, 2022–October 5, 2026 rating window unless no cutoff applies. Quinn’s exclusion from competition affects which employees remain subject to release, so I’m carefully recalculating the resulting order.**Calculating remaining positions**

I’m checking the arithmetic carefully: seven positions exist, and three are abolished, leaving four positions. Because Quinn is excluded from competition and remains in place, one of those four positions is already occupied. That leaves three positions for the six competing employees. Therefore, I’m concluding that three competing employees are retained and three are released, subject to their retention rankings and the applicable rating window.

**Calculating rating totals**

I’m calculating scores through October 5, 2026, using the applicable four-year window. Alvarez’s ratings total 19. Brandt’s performance scores total 8, plus 5 for an additional designation, making 13. Chen has two qualifying ratings; I’m using a proxy average of 6 for the missing period, producing 18. Dube has two actual ratings totaling 10, a proxy value of 5, and 3 preference points, for 18 overall. Estrada receives 3 preference points; only ratings received by October 5 count, so the later 2026 rating is excluded.**Evaluating retention periods**

I’m calculating the remaining totals and checking the restoration issue. Performance contributes 13 points, preference contributes 3, for 16 overall. Farouk has one qualifying Level 3 rating worth 3 points. The restoration question is less certain: the employee returned on July 13, 2026, after 14 months of uniformed service, and may receive either six months or one year of protection depending on the governing restoration rule. I’m not treating the duration as settled without the specific eligibility criteria or supporting rule text.

**Interpreting restoration periods**

I’m working through the applicable restoration rules, but the available text doesn’t include the full provision governing the six-month or one-year periods. The scenario’s 14 months of uniformed service likely determines which protection applies, while the stated July 13, 2026 restoration date supplies the timing context.

The final rule reproduces only part of the relevant section, even though another provision refers to the missing subsection. I’ll therefore explain the mandatory restoration protection and identify the applicable retention period cautiously, rather than claiming details the text doesn’t establish.**Assessing available authority**

I’m weighing two possibilities: the 14-month service period likely falls within the one-year restoration-protection category, while shorter qualifying service generally receives a six-month period. However, the governing subsection isn’t reproduced in the provided material, so I can’t verify its precise criteria from that source alone.

Because the scenario expressly assumes restoration under the applicable personnel rules, I can state the likely conclusion while clearly labeling the missing regulatory text as an uncertainty. I shouldn’t present remembered language as though it appears in the supplied document.
