summary.text:
**Comparing proposal changes**

I’m identifying differences between the proposed and final language that the summary may not acknowledge. One possible omission is that the proposal included “or other appropriate action” alongside a hearing, while the final version removed that phrase; the summary mentions audits, investigations, and hearings but not this narrowing.

I’m also checking a correction changing “this part” to “this subpart.” That correction affects the scope of the appeals procedures, while the summary’s broader statement that Part 351 procedures are exclusive may not capture the distinction.**Assessing unacknowledged changes**

I’m narrowing the likely omissions. The most meaningful one is the correction from “Part 351” to “this subpart,” which limits the provision’s scope, while the summary still describes Part 351 procedures broadly.

I’m also noting that the final text corrects “reconsideration of an initial appeal” to “reconsideration of an initial decision.” Other possible omissions are smaller: changing “best address” to “address,” and technical wording about withdrawing an e-filing registration and identifying the relevant representative or agency. Most other changes appear acknowledged.

**Reviewing agency changes**

I’m comparing the final rule with the proposed version and checking whether the summary captures each substantive revision. Most changes are acknowledged, including the new-matter exception, disclosure provisions, reorganized grounds, added content, initial-decision standards, factual-error review, APA applicability, participation requirements, and renumbered remedies.

One omission stands out: the summary does not clearly address the removal of “other appropriate action.” More importantly, the protective-order provision changes sanctions from mandatory (“shall”) to discretionary (“may”), except when prohibited by law. Calling this merely a refinement understates that substantive shift.**Checking remaining revisions**

I’m identifying several details that may need to be added to the comparison. The final text limits sanctions to measures that are proportionate, causally related, and no broader than necessary; describing only the protective-order limitation may miss this separate safeguard.

The summary otherwise captures reopening authority, review criteria, finality, remand procedures, director considerations, and public-posting rules, including privacy and access restrictions. I’m also noting a forum change: the final version omits one previously listed forum, adds grievance-related bars, and expressly addresses independent jurisdiction.

**Comparing appeals provisions**

I’m identifying changes between the proposed and final appeals rules that the summary may not acknowledge. One possible omission is the treatment of FLRA: the proposal expressly preserved matters within several independent forums, while the final list appears to omit FLRA without explaining that change. I’m also checking §351.904(c), where “responsible agency” may have been revised to “OPM or the agency whose action is under appeal.” These could belong in question 14(ii) as specific, unacknowledged differences.**Reviewing overlooked changes**

I’m separating terminology corrections from substantive differences, since question 14 focuses on how the final rule summarizes changes from the proposal. I’m checking whether §351.905(a), tolling under §351.902(b), and the proposal’s use of “preponderance” create additional discrepancies. The notice requirements also changed: the final rule adds timing and electronic-filing information while omitting the explicit §1201.21 reference. Finally, I’m examining the effective-scope language and possible inconsistencies with the related appellate rule.

Document number:   2026-16456
Title:             Appellate Jurisdiction Update II
Type:              Rule
Action:            Final rule.
Agencies:          Merit Systems Protection Board
Citation:          91 FR 51997
Pages:             51997-51998 (2 pages)
Published:         2026-08-12
Effective:         2026-09-02
Dates:             This final rule is effective on September 2, 2026. However, consistent with OPM's rulemakings, the MSPB will not apply this rule to pending cases or to newly filed cases relating to agency actions taken before the effective date of OPM's rulemakings, and will continue to adjudicate such probationary termination appeals, suitability appeals, and RIF appeals.
RIN:               3124-AA33
CFR affected:      5 CFR 1201
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Civil rights, Government employees
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/12/2026-16456/appellate-jurisdiction-update-ii
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-12/pdf/2026-16456.pdf

Abstract:
The Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB or Board) is amending its regulations to remove references to MSPB's jurisdiction over probationary termination, suitability, and reduction-in-force (RIF) appeals. This revision reflects the Office of Personnel Management's (OPM's) rescission of the MSPB's jurisdiction to hear these types of appeals. The rule retains MSPB's statutory jurisdiction over Foreign Service reduction-in-force appeals under 22 U.S.C. 4010a.

    41  Appellate Jurisdiction Update II
    42  
    43  AGENCY: Merit Systems Protection Board.
    44  
    45  ACTION: Final rule.
    46  
    47  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    48  
    49  SUMMARY: The Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB or Board) is amending 
    50  its regulations to remove references to MSPB's jurisdiction over 
    51  probationary termination, suitability, and reduction-in-force (RIF) 
    52  appeals. This revision reflects the Office of Personnel Management's 
    53  (OPM's) rescission of the MSPB's jurisdiction to hear these types of 
    54  appeals. The rule retains MSPB's statutory jurisdiction over Foreign 
    55  Service reduction-in-force appeals under 22 U.S.C. 4010a.
    56  
    57  DATES: This final rule is effective on September 2, 2026. However, 
    58  consistent with OPM's rulemakings, the MSPB will not apply this rule to 
    59  pending cases or to newly filed cases relating to agency actions taken 
    60  before the effective date of OPM's rulemakings, and will continue to 
    61  adjudicate such probationary termination appeals, suitability appeals, 
    62  and RIF appeals.
    63  
    64  FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Gina K. Grippando, Clerk of the Board, 
    65  Merit Systems Protection Board, 1615 M Street NW, Washington, DC 20419; 
    66  phone: (202) 653-7200; fax: (202) 653-7130; or email: [email protected].
    67  
    68  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
    69  
    70  I. Background
    71  
    72      The Civil Service Reform Act grants MSPB jurisdiction to hear 
    73  appeals of any action made appealable to MSPB under law, rule, or 
    74  regulation. 5 U.S.C. 7701(a). For the ease of MSPB's stakeholders, 
    75  MSPB's regulation at 5 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 1201.3 
    76  contains a list of the types of appeals MSPB has been granted 
    77  jurisdiction to hear. The current list includes 1201.3(a)(3), which 
    78  reflects appeal rights for employees who are terminated during their 
    79  initial or supervisory probationary period; 1201.3(a)(6), which 
    80  reflects appeals rights for employees subjected to a reduction-in-
    81  force; and 1201.3(a)(9), which reflects appeal rights for employees 
    82  subjected to a suitability action. OPM regulations previously granted 
    83  MSPB jurisdiction over each of these types of appeals, except for 
    84  reduction-in-force actions affecting a career or career candidate 
    85  appointee in the Foreign Service, over which MSPB exercises 
    86  jurisdiction pursuant to statute.
    87  
    88  A. Appeals for Terminations During Probationary or Trial Periods
    89  
    90      On June 24, 2025, OPM issued a final rule which stated that 
    91  Executive Order (E.O.) 14284, ``Strengthening Probationary Periods in 
    92  the Federal Service'' (90 FR 17729), issued on April 24, 2025, `` 
    93  `supersede[d] subpart H' [of part 315 of CFR title 5] and `rendered 
    94  [it] inoperative and without effect.' '' Accordingly, OPM's final rule 
    95  rescinded subpart H of CFR part 315, including 5 CFR 315.806, which 
    96  provided appeal rights to MSPB for employees serving an initial 
    97  appointment to a competitive service position who are terminated during 
    98  their probationary or trial period.
    99      Subsequently, effective September 2, 2026, OPM issued a final rule 
   100  revising 5 CFR 315.908(b) [of subpart I of part 315 CFR title 5] which 
   101  previously granted MSPB appeal rights to competitive service, 
   102  managerial or supervisory employees who alleged that an action under 
   103  that subpart, such as return to a nonsupervisory or nonmanagerial 
   104  position for failure to complete the probationary period, was based on 
   105  partisan political affiliation or marital status. The revised rule 
   106  rescinds MSPB appeal rights for these employees and instead provides a 
   107  right to appeal such actions to OPM.
   108      Consequently, MSPB now amends 5 CFR 1201.3(a)(3) to reflect the 
   109  rescission of these MSPB appeal rights. MSPB notes that OPM has 
   110  provided in its final rule that the rule covers actions effected from 
   111  September 2, 2026, forward, and therefore does not apply to any pending 
   112  MSPB appeals or future MSPB appeals filed based on actions effected 
   113  before September 2, 2026.
   114  
   115  B. Reduction in Force Appeals
   116  
   117      Effective September 2, 2026, OPM issued a final rule revising 5 CFR 
   118  351.901, which previously granted MSPB appeal rights to federal 
   119  employees subjected to a reduction-in-force. The new rule, in relevant 
   120  part, rescinds these MSPB appeal rights and instead provides reduction-
   121  in-force appeal rights exclusively to OPM. Consequently, MSPB now 
   122  amends 5 CFR 1201.3(a)(6) to reflect OPM's rescission of these 
   123  previously codified MSPB appeal rights. This amendment does not affect 
   124  the separate statutory right of a career or career candidate appointee 
   125  in the Foreign Service to appeal a RIF action to MSPB under 22 U.S.C. 
   126  4010a. The final rule retains that appeal right in redesignated 
   127  paragraph (a)(5) of 5 CFR 1201.3 but changes the referenced citation 
   128  from 22 U.S.C. 4011 to 22 U.S.C. 4010a, where the precise statutory 
   129  appeal reference is found.
   130      MSPB notes that OPM's final rule on RIF appeals applies only to a 
   131  RIF action for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF 
   132  notice on or after the effective date of the RIF appeals rule, and that 
   133  MSPB appeals of RIF actions taken before the effective date of OPM's 
   134  final rule may continue to be adjudicated through the MSPB process. 
   135  MSPB will therefore continue to adjudicate RIF appeals that are not 
   136  covered by OPM's final RIF appeals rule (i.e., because the RIF actions 
   137  were taken before the rule's effective date), and will accept such 
   138  cases for filing where the agency's RIF notice was issued before the 
   139  rule's effective date, and will not dismiss such appeals on the ground 
   140  that OPM's final rule displaced the MSPB's jurisdiction.
   141  
   142  C. Suitability Appeals
   143  
   144      Effective September 2, 2026, OPM issued a final rule revising 5 CFR 
   145  731.501, which previously granted MSPB appeal rights to individuals 
   146  subjected to a suitability action, which includes the cancellation of 
   147  eligibility, removal, cancellation of reinstatement eligibility, and 
   148  debarment. The new rule, in relevant part, rescinds these MSPB appeal 
   149  rights and provides suitability action appeal rights exclusively to 
   150  OPM. MSPB now amends 5 CFR 1201.3(a)(9) to reflect OPM's
   151  
   152  [[Page 51998]]
   153  
   154  rescission of these previously codified MSPB appeal rights.
   155      MSPB notes that OPM's suitability appeals rule does not apply to 
   156  suitability appeals filed with the MSPB before the effective date of 
   157  OPM's final rule, and that the MSPB may continue to adjudicate such 
   158  suitability appeals. MSPB will therefore continue to adjudicate such 
   159  suitability appeals that are not covered by OPM's final suitability 
   160  appeals rule, and will not dismiss such appeals on the ground that 
   161  OPM's final rule displaced the MSPB's jurisdiction.
   162  
   163  II. Summary of Changes
   164  
   165  Section 1201.3 Appellate Jurisdiction
   166  
   167      This amendment amends the list of appealable actions in section 
   168  1201.3(a) to remove references to appeal rights for employees in the

summary.text:
**Analyzing transition rules**

I’m identifying a potential inconsistency in the transition provisions. One passage appears to use the notice date—applying the OPM rule to notices issued on or after September 2—while another refers to the RIF’s effective date when determining MSPB jurisdiction. A separate opening provision frames the test around agency actions taken before the rule’s effective date. Applying these standards to a separation effective October 30 but noticed August 31 could produce different results, so the controlling event needs clarification.**Clarifying jurisdictional conflicts**

I’m narrowing the issue to three competing tests: the OPM appeal rule uses the notice date; another MSPB provision uses the RIF’s effective date; and the opening language refers more generally to agency action before the rule’s effective date. That creates a possible gap when notice precedes September 2 but separation occurs afterward: OPM may exclude the appeal, while MSPB’s preamble suggests continued jurisdiction. Conversely, notice after September 2 with an earlier effective date could create overlapping coverage.

**Reconciling effective dates**

I’m identifying a central inconsistency in the rule’s timing language. If notice and the effective date both precede September 2, the OPM rule does not apply, while MSPB treatment remains consistent. If notice precedes September 2 but the action becomes effective afterward, the OPM rule still does not apply under its trigger, while MSPB language based on notice and filing dates suggests it does. However, the regulatory text points to the effective date instead. I’m flagging this conflict and would cite the relevant preamble and effective-date pages.**Comparing transition triggers**

I’m tracking three possible triggers: the agency action date, the RIF notice date, and the RIF effective date. The Board’s explanatory preamble appears to use notice issuance, while another section says it will adjudicate post-September 2 appeals only when the RIF’s effective date preceded September 2. Its opening dates language also refers more generally to actions taken before the effective date. The OPM rule instead focuses on notices issued on or after September 2, creating a direct timing mismatch for cases with earlier notices but later separations.

**Resolving the jurisdiction conflict**

I’m seeing an internal contradiction in the governing text. The preamble appears to indicate that the Board would accept cases involving RIF notices issued before September 2, while Section III instead focuses on the RIF’s effective date and excludes actions effective afterward. Because the question presents notice before the date but action after it, I shouldn’t force a single confident answer. My strongest reading is that the text is unresolved: the preamble points toward MSPB jurisdiction, but the operative section points away from it.**Clarifying the transition rules**

I’m weighing whether the relevant action is the agency’s notice or the later effective date. The strongest practical answer is likely the Board, because the preamble expressly discusses notices issued before September 2, even though the operative date clause points the other way. I should present that as a likely reading, not a certainty. For the related publication questions, I’m distinguishing the principal RIF rule from its correction, the separate appeals rule, and later rules whose effective dates either precede, match, or follow September 2.

**Evaluating qualifying rules**

I’m distinguishing final rules from corrections and applying the main rule’s September 2 effective date. The September 15 correction is excluded because corrections do not count. The appeals rule, published under a separate notice, may qualify because it amends 5 CFR part 351 and shares the relevant effective date. The performance-appraisal rule is excluded because it became effective before September 2. The administrative-leave rule may qualify as published in 2026, but it is not yet effective, with an effective date of November 18.**Verifying applicability dates**

I’m checking whether the rule’s applicability turns on notices issued before September 2 versus notices issued on or after that date. The relevant dates appear in the rule’s dedicated “DATES” section, while the operative regulatory provision is likely § 351.204. I’m reviewing the opening discussion of the final rule, especially the passages around the stated dates, so I can accurately identify the controlling language and avoid relying on an incomplete paraphrase.

**Determining modal ratings**

I’m working through the proposed identification number, older comparisons, and preference-eligibility details. For the service-credit calculations, I’m treating all active-duty service as creditable where the stated provision does not exclude it, resulting in 22 years for one case and 14 years, with the appropriate subtraction, for another.

The remaining issue is Han’s modal rating. I need to rely on §351.503(f)(1), but the relevant definition appears in §351.203, which isn’t reproduced here. I’m unsure whether the five-level pattern implies a specific modal rating or requires the underlying definition.**Searching historical definitions**

I’m looking through historical Federal Register materials for the phrase “modal rating,” focusing on agency and OPM explanations. My goal is to find an explicit definition or example that clarifies how the term operates in the five-level rating pattern.

I’m searching broadly for wording such as “modal rating means,” then comparing any results with the applicable provision. This should help determine whether the modal rating is simply the most frequently assigned level or whether the regulation gives it a more specific technical meaning.

summary.text:
**Checking governing definitions**

I’m limiting the analysis to material actually printed in the relevant Federal Register documents. Although older rules may contain a definition, I can use that language only if the available records establish that later amendments did not change it. The 2026 proposal refers to “modal” as defined in §351.203 but does not revise that definition. I’m therefore checking the Federal Register history for 5 CFR part 351, rather than assuming the current Code of Federal Regulations or relying on unverified memory.**Reviewing historical text**

I’m checking the 1997 final rule to determine whether it printed the relevant definition and surrounding regulatory text. That matters because the task permits using language from older Federal Register documents when the document itself contains it. I’m also keeping the stated limitation in view: if a needed paragraph was never printed in an available document, I should not reconstruct it from memory or assume the current regulation says the same thing. The key question is whether the 1997 text supports the definition without requiring unavailable material.

Document number:   97-30428
Title:             Reduction in Force and Performance Management
Type:              Rule
Action:            Final rule.
Agencies:          Personnel Management Office
Citation:          62 FR 62495
Pages:             62495-62504 (10 pages)
Published:         1997-11-24
RIN:               3206-AH32
Significant:       True
CFR affected:      5 CFR 351, 5 CFR 430, 5 CFR 531
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/1997/11/24/97-30428/reduction-in-force-and-performance-management
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1997-11-24/pdf/97-30428.pdf

Abstract:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing final regulations that enhance the opportunity for Federal employees to receive reduction in force retention service credit based on their actual job performance. The regulations also give agencies with employees who have been rated under different patterns of summary rating levels a mechanism to take this into account when providing employees additional retention service credit for reduction in force. These regulations also clarify certain other retention rights, including the coverage of employees serving under term appointments.

summary.text:
**Verifying the modal definition**

I’m checking whether the 2026 changes altered the definition of a “modal rating” in 5 CFR 351.203. The available indications suggest that later amendments revised other definitions but did not remove or modify this provision. Accordingly, the earlier controlling rule may still apply: the modal rating is the summary level occurring most frequently among applicable ratings of record in the relevant competitive area, based on the most recently completed appraisal period before the notice or cutoff.**Determining the missing score**

I’m recognizing that Hank’s modal rating cannot be calculated from his individual history alone. Under the applicable definition, it depends on the rating occurring most frequently among employees in the relevant competitive area or agency. Because the scenario provides no distribution of those ratings, I can identify the governing formula but not a numerical result. The appropriate answer is therefore the value assigned to the applicable modal summary level, with the precise level remaining undetermined from the supplied facts.

**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m checking the final rule against the proposal, focusing on substantive rather than grammatical changes. In §351.202(c)(3), the wording changes slightly but appears non-substantive.

For §351.202(d), I’m treating the change separately. In §351.203, the furlough definition is broader in the final version: it no longer limits the shutdown exclusion to situations depending entirely on congressional action, so uncertainty at the outset may be enough. The final text also changes the probationary-period cross-reference from “§11.2 of this chapter” to “this part,” which may be an apparent drafting error.**Reviewing substantive changes**

I’m distinguishing genuine regulatory changes from simple cross-reference edits. The final text updates the rating-of-record citation, adds a “restoration-protected employee” definition, and changes the trial-period reference from “this chapter” to “this part,” creating the same possible cross-reference problem.

It also adds Merit System Principles, alternative procedures, individualized responses, and an OPM advance-approval requirement. In §351.502, the triggering date changes from when the agency issues notice to when the employee receives it across all relevant categories. Finally, §351.503 renames “Minimally Successful” as “Minimally Satisfactory” and updates related references.

**Comparing regulatory references**

I’m comparing the proposal and final language for changes in pattern references and cross-references. The final version adds a parenthetical explaining that certain patterns were authorized under §430.208(d) before the rule published at 91 FR 41521, clarifying the historical distinction rather than obviously changing the substantive scope.

I’m also noting minor edits: “this criterion” becomes “these criteria,” and paragraph (e) updates its citation from §430.208(d) to §430.208(e). These appear primarily technical and clarifying, though the historical caveat could matter for interpreting which patterns remain covered.**Reviewing cross-references**

I’m checking whether the edits change meaning or simply correct drafting. Most paragraph cross-references and rating language remain unchanged, including the option for whole-number or half-point results.

A notable correction appears in §351.505(b)(2): the final text points to §351.504(b), rather than §351.503(b), changing the referenced retiree category.

For §351.506, the final language adds more specific access limitations, clarifies that no right exists under that section while preserving rights under other laws, and refines references to employees’ performance credit and related records.

**Reviewing regulatory references**

I’m checking whether the final text of §351.701 has changed its paragraph structure. The regulatory lines still reference paragraphs (b) and (c), while paragraph (c) addresses pay rates. That means the examples’ references to assignment rights under both paragraphs may be imprecise, but not necessarily incorrect; the proposal uses the same references.

I’m also noting a possible final-rule addition involving access to records after the Privacy Act/FOIA discussion.

Separately, §351.507’s final wording says the provision remains fixed until completion of the reduction-in-force action that caused temporary retention, matching the proposal.**Comparing final revisions**

I’m identifying mostly editorial changes, including correcting “any of this paragraph (b)” to “any of these provisions.” Sections 351.601 and 351.602 remain unchanged; §351.604 removes a proposed amendment, while §§351.605 and 351.606 receive more substantial modifications. Section 351.608 mainly clarifies citations and administrative-leave wording.

In §351.701, terminology changes from “minimally successful” to “minimally satisfactory,” and a qualification reference is grammatically corrected. Section 351.702 adds a prior-job exception. Section 351.802 clarifies veterans’ preference language and record-access information, while §351.805 adds an amendment concerning delayed notice. Part 353 is also added.

**Comparing regulatory revisions**

I’m identifying only substantive differences between the proposal and final rule. I’m adding the final changes to §353.209(a) and §353.110 because they were absent from the proposal, while treating §353.301(a)’s wording change as non-substantive.

For Part 359, I’m noting the shorter furlough language and omitted congressional-dependence clause. In Part 362, I’m flagging the new recent-graduate conversion provision in §362.306. For Part 430, I’m recording the relocation from paragraph (d) to (e), removal of the fifth subparagraph, and the cross-reference change from §351.503(f) to (e).**Checking cross-references**

I’m revisiting §351.503 because the final text changes the exclusion from subsections (d) and (f) to (d) and (e). Since subsection (e) concerns multiple rating patterns while (f) concerns missing ratings, this appears potentially substantive, or possibly an unintended drafting inconsistency. I’m flagging it for verification rather than assuming the rationale.

I’m also retaining the previously identified additions and turning to the broader comparison, including authority language, notice timing, retention-register wording, and statements about employees serving probationary or trial periods.

**Assessing regulatory language**

I’m checking whether the phrase “not competing” creates any issue. At this point, I don’t see a problem. I’m also comparing the main preamble’s discussion of §351.201 erosion reclassification with the relevant wording. The key point is that the treatment is considered adverse when it occurs between the formal announcement and completion, which appears to match the text being analyzed.**Comparing regulatory text**

I’m checking the preamble against the corresponding sections for hidden discrepancies. Most descriptions appear consistent, including performance-rating rules, notice timing, retention standing, abolished competitive areas, reassignment provisions, leave and benefits coverage, rating thresholds, five-year calculations, recent ratings, and effective dates.

The main possible mismatch is in the introductory summary of §351.605. It says that abolishing an entire competitive area permits releasing employees without ranking them on a retention register or applying assignment rights. I’m flagging that wording for closer review.**Resolving apparent inconsistencies**

I’m comparing the disputed summary language with the operative provisions. Section 351.605 appears consistent: an agency may release a competing employee without regard to standing, need not rank competing employees, and must not apply assignment rights.

The executive summary’s statement about an entire competitive area being abolished also seems aligned with §351.606(a)(3): if no other competing employee can be released, the protected employee isn’t separated and is instead reassigned. I’m now checking whether the summary’s reference to tenure subgroup and service-length ties is complete.

**Checking regulatory consistency**

I’m reviewing whether the executive summary’s item about transferring reductions in force within the agency raises a genuine inconsistency. The phrase “new system of appointments” doesn’t appear relevant, so I’m setting it aside.

I’m also distinguishing between errors in explanatory examples and conflicts between the preamble and the actual regulatory text. If an example contains incorrect arithmetic but has been corrected, I shouldn’t treat that as a substantive contradiction. I’m looking for a clear mismatch between what the rule says and what the amendatory instructions establish.**Identifying discrepancies**

I’m checking whether the final text contains obvious inconsistencies rather than relying only on the examples. One possible issue is a five-year period described in the preamble as running from the reduction-in-force event, while the regulation may measure it from the notice date.

I’m also comparing statements about preference subgroups, performance ratings, and competitive-area cutoffs against the operative provisions. In particular, I’m verifying whether the preamble accurately describes the required number of ratings and the relevant timing before notice of the workforce action.

summary.text:
**Identifying regulatory inconsistencies**

I’m comparing the preamble with the regulatory text for possible contradictions. The clearest issue is in §351.507: the preamble says the relevant date is when the reduction-in-force notice is issued, while the regulation says it is when the employee receives the specific notice. Another passage in the preamble correctly uses “received,” making this a strong candidate for review.

The other provisions I’m checking—subgroup definitions, rating cutoffs, competitive-area changes, and USERRA protections—appear consistent or merely less specific.**Checking additional inconsistencies**

I’m looking for other direct mismatches between the explanatory material and the regulatory text. The strongest recurring issue remains the distinction between a notice being issued and being received, particularly for retention standing under §351.507. A similar wording issue appears in the preamble’s discussion of §351.502, where it refers generally to the RIF notice date without specifying receipt.

By contrast, the five-year period under §351.702 and the rating provisions under §351.503 appear consistent with the text.

**Ranking retention standings**

I’m calculating the total retention scores and applying the updated ranking structure. Abbott and Castillo both score 17, but Abbott has earlier seniority, so Abbott ranks first. Fontaine and Eze each score 15, followed by Dalton at 13.5 and Bianchi at 13.

That produces this order: Abbott, Castillo, Fontaine, Eze, Dalton, Bianchi. The bottom two are therefore Dalton and Bianchi. I’m also noting that military-service credit affects the seniority tie but not the total score. Under the previous rules, Bianchi’s subgroup placement could have ranked above Abbott despite lower performance.**Classifying preference groups**

I’m confirming that the earlier rules placed the 30%-disabled preference-eligible applicant in subgroup AD, above Abbott’s subgroup B. For the new scenario, the first retired officer has no preference points and remains in group B. The second has a 40% service-connected disability, but the stated retirement basis does not satisfy the required qualifying conditions, so I’m treating that person as group B as well. The third retired after 14 years because of a qualifying disability, earning five points and subgroup AD placement.

**Evaluating service credit**

I’m applying the preference and retirement rules directly. For the service member with 14 years, I’m awarding all service credit because the individual is preference-eligible under the cited provisions, producing subgroup A.

The master sergeant has 24 years of active service but does not meet the listed exceptions and receives no preference points, producing subgroup B.

The staff sergeant’s medical retirement after 16 years means retired pay is not based on 20 or more years, so the individual qualifies under the retirement exception and receives three points in subgroup A.

For the non-preference-eligible case, I’m crediting 22 active-duty years and calculating the seniority date as September 7, 1988.**Clarifying eligibility and rankings**

I’m treating the retired member as preference-eligible, so all 14 active-duty years count, producing a seniority date of September 7, 1996. A campaign badge does not limit another non-preference-eligible retired member’s credit to campaign service; all 22 years count.

The veteran subgroup identifies service records but does not independently change ranking. Preference points are added, while subgroups function mainly as tie-breakers.

For the modal rating, I can’t determine the score without the relevant appraisal distribution. Depending on the modal level, the mapping is 7, 5, 3, 0, or 0 points.

**Clarifying event dates**

I’m distinguishing three separate dates rather than treating the notice process as one event. The applicable version of the rules is determined by when the agency issues the RIF notice, specifically whether issuance occurs before or after September 2. The four-year rating-period endpoint is also tied to the notice’s issuance date, unless the agency establishes an alternative cutoff date. Finally, an employee’s tenure subgroup and retention standing are fixed when that employee receives the specific RIF notice. Using the adjusted dates, Lee is retained while Park is released.**Applying rating and appeal rules**

I’m separating the rating question from the appeal deadline. For the current rating requirement, the employee must have a Level 2 or higher annual rating, and the relevant rating is the one in effect on the release date. When comparing positions, I’m using the position occupied by the employee with the lower retention standing within the same tenure group—not the occupant’s grade intervals.

For the appeal deadline, I’m counting 30 calendar days after December 18: day 30 falls Sunday, January 17, so the deadline moves to Tuesday, January 19, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

**Clarifying filing requirements**

I’m treating question 7 as a date and calendar calculation, even though the relevant holiday isn’t in France. The filing route appears to use the OPM electronic filing system, although the materials don’t provide a direct URL. I’m checking the requirements under §§351.902(a)–(b), including the form’s contents under §351.903, a unique email address, and the deadline.

For parts (c) and (d), I’m distinguishing proof requirements and hearing rights from collective-bargaining issues. Existing agreements aren’t automatically invalidated, but direct RIF grievance or arbitration provisions may be limited.**Distinguishing review and timing**

I’m avoiding any definitive conclusion about how an existing contract should be interpreted. For judicial review, the corrected provision appears to bar court review of decisions under the relevant subpart, while leaving independent claims outside that rule.

I’m calculating the April 9 deadline by counting 30 calendar days from March 10, beginning with March 11. For the transition question, I’m comparing the notice date—not merely the action’s effective date—and noting that the applicable provisions may contain inconsistent language. I’m also reviewing the current duty-status rule’s wording.

**Clarifying administrative leave**

I’m distinguishing between the current wording, the proposed text, and the explanatory preamble. The current version uses a “when possible” requirement, while the earlier language appears to allow exceptions when work or funding is unavailable during an emergency.

For the question about administrative leave before separation, I’m relying on the preamble’s explanation of existing policy: an authorized agency official may approve administrative leave between notice and separation when justified. So my answer is yes, but only with proper agency justification and approval.**Assessing leave limits**

I’m distinguishing the new duty-default rule from the administrative-leave authority. The proposed provision allows an agency to place an employee on administrative leave for all or part of the notice period when appropriate, and the separate regulation expressly permits this when it serves the government’s best interest.

I’m also finding no stated requirement for employee consent; the preamble indicates leave may be provided with or without consent. Finally, I see no specific numerical cap in the RIF-notice provision, and the separate 12-week workforce-realignment limit may not apply to this distinct authority.

**Assessing leave and RIF limits**

I’m distinguishing between a leave provision’s duration and the separate reduction-in-force requirements. The cited provision appears to set no fixed numerical maximum; duration is generally bounded by notice requirements and applicable agency procedures. Paid leave also does not alter competitive standings, RIF competition, retention registers, or appeal rights.

For the timing issue, I’m noting that the competitive-area designation occurred August 17, while notices were issued October 13—a 57-day interval. Because the required 90-day interval and advance approval materials appear absent, the designation process seems defective despite the official chart and delegated authority.**Reviewing RIF steps**

I’m separating what can be evaluated from what the facts do not establish. The official chart may not prove that the competitive area is clearly distinguished, but the missing submission to the relevant authority is the stated defect. An excluded probationary employee appears outside the register and creates no notice issue.

The rating cutoff is September 13, so the October 2 rating cannot be used. The scoring calculation is 7 plus 5, averaged to 6, then added to 12 for 18; assigning 15 is incorrect. The QSI bonus policy also fails because it uses the wrong rating pattern and applies broadly rather than only to qualifying exceptional performance. Ties may be resolved by permitted choice.

**Assessing personnel actions**

I’m identifying several compliance issues in the sequence. The same-subgroup agency may choose among employees, but retaining Reyes in a specifically limited temporary or term promotion while releasing a competing employee appears to violate §351.602(a), because the agency must release Reyes or avoid retaining him at that level.

The exception under §351.702(a)(4)(v) may apply because he held the same position through 2023 and received a Level 4 rating in 2022 within the relevant five-year period. However, the questionnaire still appears improper if it is principally an automated self-assessment rather than a job-analysis-based assessment that lets employees demonstrate skills.

summary.text:
**Analyzing exception sequencing**

I’m comparing the cited provisions to determine whether they prohibit combining exceptions under sections 351.607 and 351.608. Section 351.606(a)(5)(iii) appears to address the agency’s authority and limits discharge, but it does not expressly impose a cross-section stacking restriction. Section 351.608(a)(3) refers specifically to exceptions under section 351.608, while section 351.607 appears to authorize an extension without stating a 90-day duration cap. The scenario may be designed to expose that ambiguity, especially regarding the additional 60 days.**Assessing duration limits**

I’m distinguishing a condition from a maximum duration. Section 351.607 appears to apply when duties cannot be transferred within 90 days, but that wording may not itself cap the exception at 90 days. Thus, a 60-day period under section 351.607 could potentially continue beyond that point if the condition remains satisfied. The additional 60 days under section 351.608(g) may still raise an anti-stacking concern, though, particularly if it effectively circumvents a general 90-day limit. The unresolved issue is whether the exceptions serve sufficiently distinct purposes.

**Interpreting exception limits**

I’m reading the provision as saying each exception operates independently and cannot be sequenced or stacked with another exception. On that reading, using the temporary §351.608(g) exception after the continuing §607 exception would likely violate §351.608(a)(3). The text does not clearly define whether the anti-stacking rule covers only multiple §351.608 exceptions, so I should present this as the strongest interpretation rather than absolute certainty. I’ll flag the additional 60-day period as noncompliant under that reading.**Checking exception details**

I’m distinguishing what the facts establish from what remains unstated. A 60-day period is within §351.608(g)’s 90-day maximum. However, “finishing a project” does not necessarily satisfy §351.607’s specific test concerning whether duties can be assumed within 90 days without undue interruption; the stated exception may imply that basis. Written notice to higher-standing employees appears required, but I can’t find noncompliance merely because the facts omit it. The appeal notice is different: directing appeals to the wrong agency and misstating the deadline makes step 12 noncompliant.

**Correcting retention calculations**

I’m updating the November 14 analysis and confirming that Question 10(a) asks specifically about September 10. The earlier calculation for Farouk was wrong: one rating at level 3 must be multiplied by three, producing 9 points rather than 3.

I’m also confirming Dube’s total as 18, Chen’s as 18, Estrada’s as 16, Alvarez’s as 19, and Brandt’s as 13. Applying the tie-breaker places Chen above Dube. The final retention order is Alvarez, Chen, Dube, Estrada, Brandt, and Farouk, making Farouk, Brandt, and Estrada the bottom three.**Applying mandatory exception**

I’m revising the release outcome: although Farouk ranks lowest on the ordinary retention register, the mandatory exception protects Farouk, so the agency must move to the next eligible employee instead. The ordinary order remains Alvarez, Chen, Dube, Estrada, Brandt, and Farouk. Therefore, the release sequence becomes Farouk passed over, followed by Brandt, Estrada, and Dube as the substitute release.

For Question 12(c), I’m checking the released employees’ current annual ratings and comparing Dube’s score of 18 with Gomez’s estimated 17 and Hill’s 14.

**Comparing retention standings**

I’m sorting the employees by retention standing and checking each position against the applicable grade limits. Gomez is the closest match, while Dube’s and Estrada’s lower-grade options are constrained by the four-level gap and their lack of qualifying disability status.

For the separate retention registers, I’m treating Gomez, Hill, Jones, and Ikeda as comparable within the same tenure group. Their calculated scores are Gomez 17, Jones 15, Hill 14, and Ikeda 9. Hill’s preference eligibility affects subgroup placement, but all four remain in career tenure group I.**Comparing assignment eligibility**

I’m comparing candidates using performance and veteran-related standing while separating retention-register placement from assignment rights. Dube remains career-conditional in subgroup II, but assignment rights still apply because the positions share the same competitive-service tenure group.

Estrada’s newer Level 5 rating does not change the result, since either the earlier Level 4 or later Level 5 satisfies the threshold. If all offers are accepted, the proposed assignments are Dube to Gomez’s position, Estrada to Hill’s, and Brandt to Ikeda’s. Quinn remains outside the competitive register, while Farouk must be retained.

**Clarifying restoration protections**

I’m distinguishing the regulation’s precise category from broader wording in the preamble. Section 351.606(a)(3) appears to apply specifically to a “restoration-protected employee”—someone restored or reemployed after uniformed service and eligible for the applicable retention period—not everyone with any restoration-related right. The preamble’s broader phrase may therefore be potentially mismatched, although another section expressly explains the narrower category. I’m also noting that the executive summary replaces the current three tenure groups with competitive and excepted groups, each having two subgroups, while excluded employees may be retained, furloughed, separated, demoted, or reassigned without RIF procedures.**Checking regulatory details**

I’m identifying several text–preamble alignment issues. One concerns the five-year assessment period: the rule measures it backward from the date the employee receives notice, while one preamble bullet refers to the RIF date; another discussion states the rule correctly. A second concerns retention standing, which freezes when the employee receives a specific RIF notice. The restoration-rights summary appears broadly consistent when read with the applicable service-protection provision. I’m also checking whether the modified notice requirement creates any conflict and noting that §351.204’s summary appears accurate.

**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m comparing the preamble’s summaries with the operative regulatory text and noting several possible inconsistencies. First, the preamble refers to the date a notice is “issued,” while the cited provisions measure the relevant period from when the employee “receives” the specific notice.

I’m also seeing a summary that describes a five-year period “of RIF,” although another analysis correctly identifies the endpoint as notice receipt. Finally, the executive summary appears narrower than §351.402(c), which covers agencies establishing or materially modifying a competitive area within 90 days before issuing notices.**Checking remaining discrepancies**

I’m reassessing the competitive-area wording and deciding not to treat the omission of “materially modified” as a contradiction. The phrase about an area being in effect for less than 90 days can reasonably describe a recently established area, while simply failing to capture every trigger in the operative text.

The ratings explanation appears consistent: both refer to the four-year period before the notice or applicable cutoff. The temporary-appointment descriptions also seem substantially aligned. I’m now turning to the table examples, where differences from the final text may reveal actual errors.

**Checking table consistency**

I’m reviewing the examples and seeing that the arithmetic appears consistent. In Example 2, performance contributes 9 points and preference adds 3, producing the displayed total of 12. Example 3 likewise shows 13 points plus 5, totaling 18, so the table appears correct.

The preamble also seems aligned with the cited provisions, including the rating definition and the five-year statement and retention date. I’m considering adding a summary bullet explaining that agencies abolishing every position in a competitive area within 180 days may release employees without ranking or assignment rights, subject to the text’s stated exceptions.**Verifying preamble differences**

I’m checking whether the executive summary’s omission of exception protections creates a conflict. It doesn’t appear to; leaving exceptions unstated doesn’t remove them from the underlying rule.

The clearer discrepancy concerns the burden described in the preamble. The regulatory text lists timeliness, jurisdiction, violation, and prejudice, while the preamble adds that the appeal must be “in required form.” That requirement may be supported separately by the filing provision, so I’m treating it as an additional explanatory condition rather than a direct contradiction, while noting the distinction carefully.

**Comparing regulatory language**

I’m checking whether the appeal preamble accurately reflects the corrected regulatory text. The timeliness burden appears to be the main point, while the added reference to proper form is implied rather than explicit.

The finality language also seems consistent: a decision becomes final when no further administrative review is available. References to OPM or the responsible agency convey the same concept as the corrected wording about the agency whose action is under appeal.

The public-posting language appears substantively unchanged; “protected personal information” looks like a typo correction. The 30-day finality summary likewise matches the rule’s requirement for a timely reopening request.**Reviewing final text**

I’m checking the final regulatory wording before reaching a conclusion. I need to compare it directly with the surrounding explanation and confirm whether the language preserves the same meaning. In particular, I’m looking for any differences involving appeal procedures, finality, timing, agency responsibility, or terminology. If the text aligns substantively, I’ll treat any remaining variation as editorial rather than a meaningful legal change. I’m holding off on a firm assessment until that comparison is complete.

**Clarifying regulatory corrections**

I’m reconciling the corrected text with the earlier draft. One wording change matters: “protected personnel” should read “protected personal information,” so I’ll use the corrected wording in Question 14.

For Question 14(i), I’m checking whether the preamble identifies only one appealable action or discusses a broader issue. The direct reference to the required form may be sufficient, but I’m comparing it with the collective-bargaining agreement discussion.

For Question 14(iii), I’m distinguishing the Board’s treatment of appeals filed after September 2 from the agency’s rule, which uses the date the notice was issued.**Organizing regulatory changes**

I’m confirming that the correction effective September 15 restored the omitted subparagraphs in the displaced-definition instruction, so Question 1(c) should reflect the corrected text.

For Question 11, I’m building a comprehensive comparison organized by provision. I’m tracking changes involving qualified assessments, CTAP and ICTAP scope, trial periods, notices, definitions, administration, triggering dates, cross-references, review access, proposal revisions, restructuring, and newly detailed protections. I’ll distinguish wording changes from substantive changes and verify each provision against both the proposed and final versions.

**Evaluating regulatory differences**

I’m sorting substantive changes from formatting-only edits in the proposed and final texts. The additions and revisions appear to involve sections 351.701–702, 351.802, 351.805, part 353, 359.802, 362.306, and 430.208, including shifted paragraphs and revised cross-references.

I’m also checking whether authority-citation changes belong in the comparison. Because the request excludes citation-format differences but includes meaningful cross-reference changes, I’m treating altered statutory authority as potentially relevant only when it changes the operative regulatory context.**Comparing substantive revisions**

I’m treating authority-citation changes as substantive when they add statutory authority that affects the rule’s legal foundation, rather than merely changing citation style. That includes additions associated with part 316 and the reduction-in-force provisions, while unchanged or reformatted citations do not count.

I’m also reviewing amendments across parts 330, 351, and 353. Some edits appear non-substantive, but others change terminology, notice timing, contact information, paragraph numbering, or cross-references. I’m paying particular attention to section 351.503, where the final text changes a cross-reference and adds a date-related qualification.

**Reviewing regulatory wording**

I’m identifying minor drafting and cross-reference issues. In §351.503(e)(1)(ii), the proposal’s “make this criteria” should be corrected to “make these criteria”; this is only a grammar change. The related references to Appendix §351.503(e)(1)(i) appear consistent, and question 11 should compare only the real provisions.

In §351.504, “must” may need to replace “should” for the subgroup requirement. Section §351.505 contains a significant cross-reference issue. For §351.506, I’m noting a substantive change: the proposal grants review rights for completed records and full registers, while the final text subjects records to applicable disclosure and privacy rules.**Comparing regulatory revisions**

I’m noting that §351.605 preserves the prior meaning while adding a separate notice paragraph and extending a mandatory exception across the full area. Sections §§351.606–351.608 appear largely consistent, with §351.606 adding detail and updated references.

For §351.701, “minimally satisfactory” replaces “minimal successful,” apparently adopting a rating descriptor without substantive change. I’m flagging additions or changes in §§351.702, 351.802, 351.805, 353.209(a), 353.110, 359.802, 362.306, and 430.208. In §330.202, revised language concerning automated self-assessments may represent a substantive criteria change.

**Comparing regulatory revisions**

I’m identifying differences between the proposed and final regulatory text. In §330.609, the final version changes “probationary or trial” to only “probationary” and cites §11.2 rather than Rule 11; it may also extend the provision to ICTAP. Section 330.707(w) appears to have a similar change.

For §330.602, I’m noting a publication issue: the final text appears to revise paragraph (1)’s introduction while omitting subparagraphs (i) and (ii), despite instructions indicating the entire paragraph should be revised. A later correction restores those provisions, making this relevant to questions 1(c) and 10.**Focusing on part 351**

I’m narrowing Q11 to 5 CFR part 351 only, excluding changes to parts 330, 353, 359, 362, and 430. The comparison should cover the amendments themselves, not the preambles, and should include every substantive difference between proposed and final text, including the authority citation if it changed.

I’m organizing the review by section and paragraph—such as §§351.202, 351.203, 351.204, 351.301, 351.302, and 351.402—and will state exactly what the proposed text said versus the final text.

**Comparing final provisions**

I’m comparing the proposed and final versions section by section, including §§351.501–507, 601–602, 604–608, 701–702, 705, 802, and the new §351.805. I’m paying particular attention to exact wording changes in §351.608 and confirming whether the new subpart belongs in the main rule. I’m also noting the expanded authority citation, which adds 5 U.S.C. §2301 and 38 U.S.C. §4331. Finally, §351.202(d) appears materially clarified: exclusions apply to competition rather than the entire part, with additional paragraphs specifying covered categories.**Analyzing employee categories**

I’m comparing the proposed and final classifications for excepted and competitive employees. The final text removes the specific notice-date qualifiers and instead focuses on whether an employee is currently serving an initial probationary or trial period. It also removes term appointments from the competitive category and places temporary appointments under the applicable subpart. I’m noting additional provisions allowing certain employees to remain and take specified actions, plus written-notice requirements. Next, I’m examining §351.203, including whether the final rule broadens the furlough exclusion.

**Comparing regulatory revisions**

Q7.answer:
(a) The OPM process does not apply to an August 31 notice, because the appeals rule applies only when the agency issues the specific RIF notice on or after September 2. The Board’s preamble expressly says it will accept MSPB RIF appeals when the agency’s notice preceded that date, so MSPB is the best-supported forum on that passage. But the Board’s own effective-date discussion also says it will hear post-September 2 appeals only when the RIF effective date preceded September 2; Morgan’s October 30 effective date fails that test. The 2026 documents therefore conflict for this precise notice/effective-date combination; the forum cannot be stated with certainty from the Federal Register alone.
(b) OPM hears the appeal. It must be filed through the electronic filing system identified on OPM’s website. Count December 19 as day 1: December 19–31 = 13 days; January 1–17 = 17 more, day 30 is Sunday, January 17, 2027. January 18 is a Federal holiday, so the filing period extends to Tuesday, January 19, 2027, by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.
(c) By a preponderance of the evidence, Morgan must establish timeliness, OPM jurisdiction, an agency failure to comply with an applicable RIF statute or OPM regulation, and prejudice—causing the appealed action or loss of a materially more favorable outcome. She is not entitled to a hearing as of right. OPM uses the written record unless it finds a hearing necessary and efficient, including where a material fact is undeveloped or a material credibility issue is disputed.
(d) The rule makes the OPM procedures the exclusive means of directly appealing a covered RIF and bars raising the RIF action or appeal-related matter through a negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration. The preamble says OPM is not retroactively invalidating existing CBAs in this rulemaking; effects of particular existing provisions and related chapter 71 disputes remain for the appropriate forum. The preamble says that when agreements are renegotiated, the rule limits bargaining for a conflicting direct RIF-appeal process.
(e) No party may obtain judicial review of an OPM decision under the RIF-appeal subpart. The rule does not purport to remove independent collateral claims assigned to other forums.
(f) Yes, subject to OPM’s determination that the final OSC decision materially affects her rights under part 351. The decision is final March 10, 2027; count March 11 as day 1. March 11–31 = 21 days and April 1–9 = 9 days, making April 9, 2027 the 30th day to file.
(g) The OPM appeals rule’s DATES provision states that the new process applies only to an action for which the agency issues the employee a specific notice under §351.802 on or after September 2, 2026. That is the event distinguishing the two notice dates. The MSPB rule’s conflicting language is addressed in (a).
Q7.uncertainty: The Board’s preamble applies the transition by notice issuance (91 FR 51997), while its effective-date discussion applies it by the RIF effective date (91 FR 51998). Morgan’s August 31 notice and October 30 separation fall on opposite sides of those tests.

Q9.answer:
(1) **Does not comply.** The office is an organizational unit on the chart and the designation was approved by the agency head’s designee, but it was established August 17, only 57 days before October 13. An area established or materially modified within 90 days before notices requires submission of its description and written bona fide organizational basis to OPM for advance approval. Tulsa must submit those materials and obtain approval.
(2) **In order.** A career-conditional employee still in the initial probationary period is not a competing employee; the agency may retain her while releasing a competing employee.
(3) **Does not comply.** Career tenure and a supervisory probationary period do not exclude Ortiz. “Initial probationary period” expressly excludes the probationary period on initial appointment to a supervisory/managerial position. Ortiz must be treated as a competing employee and ranked in her tenure subgroup.
(4) **Does not comply.** Thirty days before October 13 is September 13. The October 2 rating was put on record after the cutoff and cannot be used, even if signed and issued and favorable to Pruitt. Use the ratings allowed by the September 13 cutoff.
(5) **Does not comply.** Level 5=7 and Level 4=5; proxy=(7+5)/2=6; Quist’s credit is 7+5+6=18, not 7+5+3=15.
(6) **Does not comply.** Additional exceptional-performance credit under the single-pattern provision is available only when the highest level of the pattern is Level 3, and then is for Level 3 employees with qualifying exceptional performance. A five-level pattern does not qualify, and a QSI does not authorize adding two points to every recipient regardless of rating. Advance written policy does not cure those limits.
(7) **In order.** With identical augmented performance credit, tenure subgroup, and service date, the employees are tied for release and the agency may select either.
(8) **Does not comply.** The agency may not release a competing employee while retaining in that level an employee with a specifically limited temporary or term promotion. The temporary promotion ending in March 2027 falls within that prohibition; the agency must not retain Reyes in that level while releasing the competing employee.
(9) **In order.** The agency need not administer an assignment assessment if, within the five-year period ending on notice receipt, the employee occupied the same position and received Level 3 or higher for those duties. Silva’s stated same-position service through 2023 and Level 4 in 2022 meet that exception for an October 13, 2026 notice.
(10) **Does not comply.** An assignment assessment must allow demonstration of job-related skills and be based on job analysis; it may not consist solely of or principally rely on an automated self-assessment. The questionnaire described is disallowed. Use a compliant assessment unless an exception applies.
(11) **The first 60 days may qualify; the additional 60 days are not supportable as stated.** Section 351.607 permits a continuing exception for duties that cannot be taken over within 90 days without undue interruption, with written notice to each higher-standing employee reached for release. Section 351.608(a)(3) prohibits sequencing or stacking an exception under that section with another exception and permits choosing the longest applicable period. The text does not expressly explain whether that bar also reaches a §351.607 continuing exception followed by a §351.608(g) temporary exception; the safest reading is not to stack them. If the agency uses §351.607, it must satisfy its duty/notice conditions; it cannot simply add a further §351.608(g) period without resolving that textual scope issue.
(12) **Does not comply.** For an October 13 notice, the applicable appeal is to OPM, not MSPB, and the notice must state the OPM appeal right, deadline, and electronic filing system. Correct the notice language.

Q10.answer:
(a) On September 10, paragraph (1) of “displaced” contained the revised introductory text—an eligible current competitive-service employee in the competitive-service tenure group at GS-15 or below (or another qualifying appointment), “who:” —but the two subparagraphs specifying the qualifying circumstances were absent. Q11.answer:
Comparing the **part 351 regulatory amendments**, the real differences I find are:

1. **Part 351 authority citation.** The proposal cited 5 U.S.C. 1302, 3502, and 3503; the final also cites 5 U.S.C. 2301 and 38 U.S.C. 4331.
2. **§351.202(c)(3), (d).** The final corrects the proposal’s wording in (c)(3). More substantively, the proposal said the listed employees were excluded from part 351 and could be dealt with “without regard” to it. The final instead says they are not “competing employees,” explains that the agency may act without determining their standing, applying release order, or giving assignment rights, and adds a written-notice requirement for specified actions. The final also drops the express “as of the notice date” wording for trial/initial-probationary status; removes competitive-service term appointments and part 316, subpart C from the short-appointment exclusion; and limits that competitive-service exclusion to temporary appointments under subpart D.
3. **§351.203.** The final adds “restoration protected employee,” absent from the proposal. It changes the emergency-shutdown furlough exclusion by deleting the proposal’s added requirement that the unknown duration be entirely dependent on congressional, rather than agency, action. It changes the “initial probationary period” cross-reference from §11.2 “of this chapter” to §11.2 “of this part,” and likewise changes the trial-period cross-reference from §11.3 “of this chapter” to “of this part.” The rating-of-record definition changes its part 430 cross-reference from §430.208(d) to §430.208(e) and makes wording changes.
4. **§351.204.** The final adds the agency’s duty to ensure the rules are administered consistently with applicable law, including the merit-system principles in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b); the proposal ended after the duty to follow and apply part 351.
5. **§351.302(d), (g).** The final adds that part 752 procedures apply “if applicable” and that other procedures required by law, regulation, or appointment terms may govern separation. The canvass language changes from asking whether “employees” prefer transfer and giving “the employee” information to asking each employee and giving each the information.
6. **§351.402.** The final adds paragraph (c): an area established or materially modified within 90 days before notices requires submission of the description and written bona fide organizational basis to OPM for advance approval. The proposal amended paragraph (b) only.
7. **§351.502(a)(2)–(3), (b)(2)–(3).** The proposal measured status on the date the agency **issues** the specific notice; the final uses the date the employee **receives** it.
8. **§351.503.** The final updates references to rating patterns from §430.208(d) to §430.208(e), changes the Level 2 descriptor from “Minimally Successful” to “Minimally Satisfactory,” and adds the historical qualification for pattern D and patterns B/E/F/H tied to the later performance-appraisal rule. These are changes in the pattern reference/description, not punctuation.
9. **§351.504(a)(1)–(3).** The proposal said preference subgroups “should be identified”; the final says they “must be identified.”
10. **§351.505(b)(2).** The proposal limited the retired-member service-credit provision by referring to employees covered by §351.503(b); the final corrects the cross-reference to §351.504(b), the veterans’-preference provision.
11. **§351.506(d).** The final says the no-review rule is only a limit on access “under this section” and does not limit access available under another statute or regulation; the proposal had no such saving sentence.
12. **§351.604.** The proposal would revise paragraph (b)’s written furlough/recall criteria and remove paragraph (d). The final does not finalize that amendment and leaves §351.604 unchanged.
13. **§351.605.** The final separates the notice rules into paragraph (c) and the no-register/no-assignment-rights rule into paragraph (d). It expressly requires a written notice under §351.801, identifies its required and omitted §351.802 content, and states that no register is required and assignment rights must not be applied. The proposal placed notice language within paragraph (b) and did not add the separate paragraph (d).
14. **§351.606(a).** The proposal addressed the order under §351.601 and stated a priority for employees protected under a cited §351.209(b). The final applies the mandatory exception under §§351.601 **and** 351.605, cites §353.209(b), specifies pass-over and reassignment when an area is abolished, provides for OPM placement assistance in stated circumstances, and requires documentation. The final also revises §351.606(c) from “shall” to “shall”/inspection language? The substantive additional material is in (a).
15. **§351.608(a)(2).** The CTAP cross-reference changes from part 330, subpart E, in the proposal to subpart F in the final.
16. **§351.701.** The final changes the Level 2 descriptor from “minimally successful” to “minimally satisfactory.” It reorganizes the provision into “General,” “Assignment rights,” and “Pay rates” paragraphs; the core three-/five-grade rule and related grade-progression provisions remain substantially the same.
17. **§351.702(a)(4).** The automated-assessment test is rephrased: proposal, “does not solely include or principally rely on a self-assessment from an automated examination”; final, “does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment.” The final also adds paragraph (v), excusing an assessment when the employee recently performed the same or substantially equivalent work and received Level 3 or higher within the five-year period ending on notice receipt.
18. **§351.802(a), (a)(2)–(3).** The final adds the introductory requirement that a specific written §351.801 notice must include the listed items, except as otherwise provided in part 351. It changes “veteran status” to “veterans’ preference subgroup,” and changes the records language from access to the agency’s records to information on how to access them.
19. **§351.805(b).** The final adds a rule that an amended notice stating only a later effective date is not a new specific notice for §351.507 and does not require recalculation of standing; the proposal did not amend this paragraph.
Q11.basis: Proposed amendments: 2026-04377, 91 FR 10926–10934, especially part 351 at 10926–10934. Final amendments: 2026-15665, 91 FR 49218–49226, especially §§351.202–.805. Q11.uncertainty: The proposal and final contain several minor wording edits in addition to the substantive differences listed. I have not treated grammatical, punctuation, or mere citation-format edits as separate differences.

Q12.answer:
(a) Quinn is not on the register: a career-conditional employee in the initial probationary period is excluded from RIF competition. Scores for the competing employees: Alvarez 7+7+5=19, +0=19; Brandt 3+5+0=8, +5=13; Chen’s September 30, 2022 Level 2 is outside the four-year period ending October 5, 2026; her two actual ratings are 7 and 5, proxy=(7+5)/2=6, so 7+5+6=18, +0=18; Dube’s two Level 4 ratings are 5+5=10, proxy=5, so 15, +3=18; Estrada’s October 20 rating is after the October 5 notice and is not used, so 5+3+5=13, +3=16; Farouk has one Level 3 rating, so 3×3=9, +0=9. Ikeda is four intervals below and out of range. Brandt has current Level 2 and the 30%-disabled preference-eligible five-interval limit. Q12.basis: 2026-15665, §§351.202(d)(2)(ii), 351.502(a), 351.503(a), (c), (f)(2)–(3), 351.504(a), 351.501(c), 91 FR 49218–49223; restoration protection and pass-over, §351.606(a), 91 FR 49223–49224 and preamble 91 FR 49203; assignment rights, §§351.701–.702, 91 FR 49225–49226. Q13.answer:
I find these checked preamble/text mismatches:

1. **Standing trigger—issued versus received.** The preamble says that standing is frozen on the date the RIF notice “is issued” (91 FR 49185). The regulatory text says standing is determined on the date the employee “receives a specific reduction in force notice” (§351.507(a)–(b), 91 FR 49223). A later passage correctly says “receives” (91 FR 49179, Executive Summary item 16; also 91 FR 49202, §351.805 discussion).
2. **Five-year assessment exception.** The Executive Summary describes the assessment exemption as applying if the employee held the same/similar position “within five years of the RIF” (91 FR 49179, item 13). The text specifies a five-year period **ending on the date the employee receives** the specific RIF notice (§351.702(a)(4)(v), 91 FR 49226). The section-by-section discussion states the notice-receipt endpoint correctly (91 FR 49205, §351.702 discussion).

I do not count a preamble omission of a regulatory detail as a mismatch, and I do not find a separate confirmed contradiction in the other section summaries checked.
Q13.uncertainty: The preamble’s phrase “within five years of the RIF” is imprecise; the operative text supplies the exact five-year endpoint.

Q14.answer:
(i) **Preamble/text differences in OPM’s appeals rule.** First, the preamble says §351.901(c) makes the procedures in “part 351” the sole and exclusive means of appeal (2026-15666, 91 FR 49244). As corrected, §351.901(c)(1) says the procedures in “this subpart” are the exclusive means (2026-17338, 91 FR 54796 correcting 2026-15666, 91 FR 49263). Second, the section analysis says the appellant must prove that the appeal was timely “and in the required form” (2026-15666, 91 FR 49248); §351.901(b)(1) lists timeliness, but not a separate burden element of proper form, while §351.903(a) separately states the appeal’s form/content requirements (91 FR 49263–49264). Third, the preamble summary says public posting is limited to protect “protected personnel information” (91 FR 49231); the correction changes the regulatory phrase to “protected personal information” (§351.909(f), 2026-17338, 91 FR 54796 correcting 2026-15666, 91 FR 49267).

(ii) **Proposal-to-final differences not acknowledged in the summary of changes.** (1) The final/corrected §351.901(c)(1) changes “this part” in the proposal to “this subpart”; the summary still describes the exclusive process as part 351 procedures. (2) §351.902(a) changes the filing object from reconsideration of an “initial appeal” under “this part” to reconsideration of an “initial decision” under “this subpart”; the summary does not identify that correction. (3) §351.901(c)(3) omits the Federal Labor Relations Authority from the proposed list of collateral forums, while the summary lists the final forums but does not call out the deletion. (4) §351.903(b) changes the agency-response deadline from “within 30 calendar days of the initial appeal” to “within 30 calendar days after service,” with a separate rule that the 30 days begin upon service; the summary does not mention that trigger clarification. (5) §351.905(c) removes the proposal’s authority to direct “any other appropriate action” and retains the more specific fact-development tools; the summary discusses narrowing audits/investigations but does not mention deleting that authority. (6) §351.906(b) changes mandatory sanctions (“OPM shall”) to discretionary sanctions (“OPM may”), and final §351.906(c) adds that sanctions must be proportionate, causally related, and no broader than necessary; the summary’s protective-order discussion does not identify either change.

(iii) The MSPB rule has conflicting transition statements. Its DATES text says it will not apply the rule to pending or newly filed cases concerning agency actions taken before the effective date of OPM’s rulemakings and will continue to hear those RIF appeals (2026-16456, 91 FR 51997). Its RIF preamble says MSPB will accept appeals where the agency issued the RIF notice before September 2 (91 FR 51997). But its later “Effective Date of Amendment” section says MSPB will adjudicate RIF appeals received after September 2 only where the RIF effective date preceded September 2 (91 FR 51998). OPM’s appeals rule, in turn, makes its process apply by **notice issuance** on or after September 2 (2026-15666, 91 FR 49230, DATES). Thus a pre-September 2 notice with a post-September 2 effective date is treated differently by the MSPB preamble and its later effective-date statement.
Q14.basis: OPM proposal: 2026-02576, 91 FR 5861–5877; OPM final rule: 2026-15666, 91 FR 49230–49267; OPM correction: 2026-17338, 91 FR 54796; MSPB final rule: 2026-16456, 91 FR 51997–51998. The corrections quoted above are part of the regulatory text as of November 14, 2026.
Q14.uncertainty: The MSPB transition inconsistency leaves the Board’s treatment of a pre-effective-date notice with a later effective separation unclear. The items in (i) are textual discrepancies, not conclusions about their legal effect.

Q3.answer:
(a) A: not preference eligible; 0 points; subgroup B.
