GS-9 Hana is four grade intervals below; GS-12 Ito has higher standing; part-time GS-12 Kim has a different schedule; and GS-12 Lund is outside the competitive area. None of those is available under the stated rule.
(b) With a compensable service-connected disability of at least 30%, the limit becomes five grades/intervals. Hana’s GS-9 position becomes within range, but Ellis’s GS-12 position remains the least reduction and is still the required offer.
(c) With a current annual Level 1 rating, Jordan does not meet the Level 2-or-higher threshold; §351.701 does not require an assignment offer under these provisions.
(d) If all are in the excepted service, §351.701 does not give Jordan the competitive-service assignment right. An agency may choose to provide excepted-service assignment rights under §351.705(a), on the same basis and under the same appointing authority; the scenario does not say it has done so.
(e) The old handbook’s higher-rating rule and its bump/retreat distinction do not state the 2026 rule. Assignment turns on whether the holder has lower retention standing in the same tenure group—not on a comparison of the two employees’ current ratings alone. OPM says the new rule eliminates the separate bump/retreat concepts and successive rounds of those procedures.
Q6.basis: 2026-15665, 5 CFR 351.701(a)–(d), 91 FR 49225–49226; §351.702(a)(4), 91 FR 49226; §351.705(a), 91 FR 49226. Preamble discussion of the replacement of bump/retreat is at 91 FR 49204.
Q6.uncertainty: Excepted-service assignment rights are discretionary under §351.705(a); the scenario does not establish an agency policy granting them.

Q7.answer:
(a) The OPM process does not apply to an August 31 notice, because the appeals rule applies only when the agency issues the specific RIF notice on or after September 2. The Board’s preamble expressly says it will accept MSPB RIF appeals when the agency’s notice preceded that date, so MSPB is the best-supported forum on that passage. But the Board’s own effective-date discussion also says it will hear post-September 2 appeals only when the RIF effective date preceded September 2; Morgan’s October 30 effective date fails that test. The 2026 documents therefore conflict for this precise notice/effective-date combination; the forum cannot be stated with certainty from the Federal Register alone.
(b) OPM hears the appeal. It must be filed through the electronic filing system identified on OPM’s website. Count December 19 as day 1: December 19–31 = 13 days; January 1–17 = 17 more, day 30 is Sunday, January 17, 2027. January 18 is a Federal holiday, so the filing period extends to Tuesday, January 19, 2027, by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.
(c) By a preponderance of the evidence, Morgan must establish timeliness, OPM jurisdiction, an agency failure to comply with an applicable RIF statute or OPM regulation, and prejudice—causing the appealed action or loss of a materially more favorable outcome. She is not entitled to a hearing as of right. OPM uses the written record unless it finds a hearing necessary and efficient, including where a material fact is undeveloped or a material credibility issue is disputed.
(d) The rule makes the OPM procedures the exclusive means of directly appealing a covered RIF and bars raising the RIF action or appeal-related matter through a negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration. The preamble says OPM is not retroactively invalidating existing CBAs in this rulemaking; effects of particular existing provisions and related chapter 71 disputes remain for the appropriate forum. The preamble says that when agreements are renegotiated, the rule limits bargaining for a conflicting direct RIF-appeal process.
(e) No party may obtain judicial review of an OPM decision under the RIF-appeal subpart. The rule does not purport to remove independent collateral claims assigned to other forums.
(f) Yes, subject to OPM’s determination that the final OSC decision materially affects her rights under part 351. The decision is final March 10, 2027; count March 11 as day 1. March 11–31 = 21 days and April 1–9 = 9 days, making April 9, 2027 the 30th day to file.
(g) The OPM appeals rule’s DATES provision states that the new process applies only to an action for which the agency issues the employee a specific notice under §351.802 on or after September 2, 2026. That is the event distinguishing the two notice dates. The MSPB rule’s conflicting language is addressed in (a).
Q7.uncertainty: The Board’s preamble applies the transition by notice issuance (91 FR 51997), while its effective-date discussion applies it by the RIF effective date (91 FR 51998). Morgan’s August 31 notice and October 30 separation fall on opposite sides of those tests.

Q8.answer:
(a) On November 14 the not-yet-replaced §351.806 version applies: OPM described it as directing that the employee remain in duty status “when possible.” The adopted replacement, effective November 18, says under ordinary circumstances an employee remains in duty status during the notice period, and separately permits administrative leave when appropriate and consistent with part 630, subpart N.
(b) Under the adopted text, employee consent is not required for administrative leave. Section 351.806(b) permits leave for all or part of the notice period; §630.1403(c)(10) identifies RIF notice-period leave as an acceptable use when the agency determines it is in the Government’s best interests. Those provisions state no fixed numerical limit for this RIF-notice use; the leave cannot extend beyond the notice period under §351.806(b) and remains subject to part 630, subpart N. The separate 12-week policy limit described for certain workforce-realignment initiatives is not stated in §630.1403(c)(10) as a limit on this RIF-notice use.
(c) OPM says that, before the regulation takes effect, existing OPM policy guidance already allowed an authorized agency official to provide administrative leave between receipt of an involuntary-separation notice and its effective date.
(d) Administrative leave does not alter retention standing, RIF competition, notice requirements, or appeal rights. OPM says the RIF rules continue to apply in full and the change does not authorize bypassing retention registers or appeal rights.
Q8.basis: Proposed rule description of then-current §351.806: 2026-13073, 91 FR 39034; final rule DATES and preamble: 2026-21320, 91 FR 65924, 65926, 65933; adopted §351.806(a)–(c), 91 FR 65939; §630.1403(a)(3), (c)(10), 91 FR 65939–65940.
Q8.uncertainty: The 2026 proposal and final rule describe, but do not reprint, the complete pre-November 18 version of §351.806. The answer states only the duty-status standard shown in those documents.

Q9.answer:
(1) **Does not comply.** The office is an organizational unit on the chart and the designation was approved by the agency head’s designee, but it was established August 17, only 57 days before October 13. An area established or materially modified within 90 days before notices requires submission of its description and written bona fide organizational basis to OPM for advance approval. Tulsa must submit those materials and obtain approval.
(2) **In order.** A career-conditional employee still in the initial probationary period is not a competing employee; the agency may retain her while releasing a competing employee.
(3) **Does not comply.** Career tenure and a supervisory probationary period do not exclude Ortiz. “Initial probationary period” expressly excludes the probationary period on initial appointment to a supervisory/managerial position. Ortiz must be treated as a competing employee and ranked in her tenure subgroup.
(4) **Does not comply.** Thirty days before October 13 is September 13. The October 2 rating was put on record after the cutoff and cannot be used, even if signed and issued and favorable to Pruitt. Use the ratings allowed by the September 13 cutoff.
(5) **Does not comply.** Level 5=7 and Level 4=5; proxy=(7+5)/2=6; Quist’s credit is 7+5+6=18, not 7+5+3=15.
(6) **Does not comply.** Additional exceptional-performance credit under the single-pattern provision is available only when the highest level of the pattern is Level 3, and then is for Level 3 employees with qualifying exceptional performance. A five-level pattern does not qualify, and a QSI does not authorize adding two points to every recipient regardless of rating. Advance written policy does not cure those limits.
(7) **In order.** With identical augmented performance credit, tenure subgroup, and service date, the employees are tied for release and the agency may select either.
(8) **Does not comply.** The agency may not release a competing employee while retaining in that level an employee with a specifically limited temporary or term promotion. The temporary promotion ending in March 2027 falls within that prohibition; the agency must not retain Reyes in that level while releasing the competing employee.
(9) **In order.** The agency need not administer an assignment assessment if, within the five-year period ending on notice receipt, the employee occupied the same position and received Level 3 or higher for those duties. Silva’s stated same-position service through 2023 and Level 4 in 2022 meet that exception for an October 13, 2026 notice.
(10) **Does not comply.** An assignment assessment must allow demonstration of job-related skills and be based on job analysis; it may not consist solely of or principally rely on an automated self-assessment. The questionnaire described is disallowed. Use a compliant assessment unless an exception applies.
(11) **The first 60 days may qualify; the additional 60 days are not supportable as stated.** Section 351.607 permits a continuing exception for duties that cannot be taken over within 90 days without undue interruption, with written notice to each higher-standing employee reached for release. Section 351.608(a)(3) prohibits sequencing or stacking an exception under that section with another exception and permits choosing the longest applicable period. The text does not expressly explain whether that bar also reaches a §351.607 continuing exception followed by a §351.608(g) temporary exception; the safest reading is not to stack them. If the agency uses §351.607, it must satisfy its duty/notice conditions; it cannot simply add a further §351.608(g) period without resolving that textual scope issue.
(12) **Does not comply.** For an October 13 notice, the applicable appeal is to OPM, not MSPB, and the notice must state the OPM appeal right, deadline, and electronic filing system. Correct the notice language.
Q9.uncertainty: Step 11 has a scope ambiguity: §351.608(a)(3) expressly addresses exceptions under that section but also says they may not be combined with “another exception”; it does not expressly discuss §351.607.

Q10.answer:
(a) On September 10, paragraph (1) of “displaced” contained the revised introductory text—an eligible current competitive-service employee in the competitive-service tenure group at GS-15 or below (or another qualifying appointment), “who:” —but the two subparagraphs specifying the qualifying circumstances were absent. As published, the definition therefore did not state those circumstances.
(b) On September 15, FR Doc. 2026-18800 restored paragraph (1)(i) (receipt of a RIF separation notice, unless the employee declined a qualifying same-schedule offer at least as high in representative rate) and paragraph (1)(ii) (certain proposed removals for declining a directed geographic relocation). OPM said it acted without notice and comment because the correction restored text it had not intended to remove, made no substantive change, and had good cause; it characterized the change as correcting an inadvertent amendatory-instruction error.
(c) After correction, a full-time offer at a lower representative rate is not an offer “at least as high” as Nadia’s current rate. If she declines it, she remains displaced under paragraph (1)(i). If the offered full-time position has the same representative rate, and she declines it, she is no longer displaced under paragraph (1)(i), because the offer is at least as high and has the same schedule.
Q10.basis: 2026-15665, 91 FR 49217, amendatory instruction 11; 2026-18800, 91 FR 58363–58364, especially the explanation of the omission and corrected §330.602 paragraph (1)(i)–(ii).

Q11.answer:
Comparing the **part 351 regulatory amendments**, the real differences I find are:

1. **Part 351 authority citation.** The proposal cited 5 U.S.C. 1302, 3502, and 3503; the final also cites 5 U.S.C. 2301 and 38 U.S.C. 4331.
2. **§351.202(c)(3), (d).** The final corrects the proposal’s wording in (c)(3). More substantively, the proposal said the listed employees were excluded from part 351 and could be dealt with “without regard” to it. The final instead says they are not “competing employees,” explains that the agency may act without determining their standing, applying release order, or giving assignment rights, and adds a written-notice requirement for specified actions. The final also drops the express “as of the notice date” wording for trial/initial-probationary status; removes competitive-service term appointments and part 316, subpart C from the short-appointment exclusion; and limits that competitive-service exclusion to temporary appointments under subpart D.
3. **§351.203.** The final adds “restoration protected employee,” absent from the proposal. It changes the emergency-shutdown furlough exclusion by deleting the proposal’s added requirement that the unknown duration be entirely dependent on congressional, rather than agency, action. It changes the “initial probationary period” cross-reference from §11.2 “of this chapter” to §11.2 “of this part,” and likewise changes the trial-period cross-reference from §11.3 “of this chapter” to “of this part.” The rating-of-record definition changes its part 430 cross-reference from §430.208(d) to §430.208(e) and makes wording changes.
4. **§351.204.** The final adds the agency’s duty to ensure the rules are administered consistently with applicable law, including the merit-system principles in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b); the proposal ended after the duty to follow and apply part 351.
5. **§351.302(d), (g).** The final adds that part 752 procedures apply “if applicable” and that other procedures required by law, regulation, or appointment terms may govern separation. The canvass language changes from asking whether “employees” prefer transfer and giving “the employee” information to asking each employee and giving each the information.
6. **§351.402.** The final adds paragraph (c): an area established or materially modified within 90 days before notices requires submission of the description and written bona fide organizational basis to OPM for advance approval. The proposal amended paragraph (b) only.
7. **§351.502(a)(2)–(3), (b)(2)–(3).** The proposal measured status on the date the agency **issues** the specific notice; the final uses the date the employee **receives** it.
8. **§351.503.** The final updates references to rating patterns from §430.208(d) to §430.208(e), changes the Level 2 descriptor from “Minimally Successful” to “Minimally Satisfactory,” and adds the historical qualification for pattern D and patterns B/E/F/H tied to the later performance-appraisal rule. These are changes in the pattern reference/description, not punctuation.
9. **§351.504(a)(1)–(3).** The proposal said preference subgroups “should be identified”; the final says they “must be identified.”
10. **§351.505(b)(2).** The proposal limited the retired-member service-credit provision by referring to employees covered by §351.503(b); the final corrects the cross-reference to §351.504(b), the veterans’-preference provision.
11. **§351.506(d).** The final says the no-review rule is only a limit on access “under this section” and does not limit access available under another statute or regulation; the proposal had no such saving sentence.
12. **§351.604.** The proposal would revise paragraph (b)’s written furlough/recall criteria and remove paragraph (d). The final does not finalize that amendment and leaves §351.604 unchanged.
13. **§351.605.** The final separates the notice rules into paragraph (c) and the no-register/no-assignment-rights rule into paragraph (d). It expressly requires a written notice under §351.801, identifies its required and omitted §351.802 content, and states that no register is required and assignment rights must not be applied. The proposal placed notice language within paragraph (b) and did not add the separate paragraph (d).
14. **§351.606(a).** The proposal addressed the order under §351.601 and stated a priority for employees protected under a cited §351.209(b). The final applies the mandatory exception under §§351.601 **and** 351.605, cites §353.209(b), specifies pass-over and reassignment when an area is abolished, provides for OPM placement assistance in stated circumstances, and requires documentation. The final also revises §351.606(c) from “shall” to “shall”/inspection language? The substantive additional material is in (a).
15. **§351.608(a)(2).** The CTAP cross-reference changes from part 330, subpart E, in the proposal to subpart F in the final.
16. **§351.701.** The final changes the Level 2 descriptor from “minimally successful” to “minimally satisfactory.” It reorganizes the provision into “General,” “Assignment rights,” and “Pay rates” paragraphs; the core three-/five-grade rule and related grade-progression provisions remain substantially the same.
17. **§351.702(a)(4).** The automated-assessment test is rephrased: proposal, “does not solely include or principally rely on a self-assessment from an automated examination”; final, “does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment.” The final also adds paragraph (v), excusing an assessment when the employee recently performed the same or substantially equivalent work and received Level 3 or higher within the five-year period ending on notice receipt.
18. **§351.802(a), (a)(2)–(3).** The final adds the introductory requirement that a specific written §351.801 notice must include the listed items, except as otherwise provided in part 351. It changes “veteran status” to “veterans’ preference subgroup,” and changes the records language from access to the agency’s records to information on how to access them.
19. **§351.805(b).** The final adds a rule that an amended notice stating only a later effective date is not a new specific notice for §351.507 and does not require recalculation of standing; the proposal did not amend this paragraph.
Q11.basis: Proposed amendments: 2026-04377, 91 FR 10926–10934, especially part 351 at 10926–10934. Final amendments: 2026-15665, 91 FR 49218–49226, especially §§351.202–.805. Correction to the separate part 330 CTAP amendment: 2026-18800, 91 FR 58363–58364. This comparison excludes punctuation/capitalization and citation-format-only changes.
Q11.uncertainty: The proposal and final contain several minor wording edits in addition to the substantive differences listed. I have not treated grammatical, punctuation, or mere citation-format edits as separate differences.

Q12.answer:
(a) Quinn is not on the register: a career-conditional employee in the initial probationary period is excluded from RIF competition. Scores for the competing employees: Alvarez 7+7+5=19, +0=19; Brandt 3+5+0=8, +5=13; Chen’s September 30, 2022 Level 2 is outside the four-year period ending October 5, 2026; her two actual ratings are 7 and 5, proxy=(7+5)/2=6, so 7+5+6=18, +0=18; Dube’s two Level 4 ratings are 5+5=10, proxy=5, so 15, +3=18; Estrada’s October 20 rating is after the October 5 notice and is not used, so 5+3+5=13, +3=16; Farouk has one Level 3 rating, so 3×3=9, +0=9. The ordinary register order is Alvarez (19), Chen (18), Dube (18), Estrada (16), Brandt (13), Farouk (9). Chen precedes Dube on their tie because Chen is tenure subgroup I and Dube, career-conditional after probation, is subgroup II.
(b) Farouk’s 14 months of uniformed service is over 180 days. The main-rule preamble describes a one-year post-reemployment protection for service over 180 days. Farouk was restored July 13, 2026, and remains within that period on the October 5 notice date. Under the mandatory exception, the agency passes over Farouk and releases the next lower-standing employee instead. The three employees released from the GS-13 level are Dube, Estrada, and Brandt; Quinn is excluded, and Farouk is protected.
(c) Assignment comparisons for the four lower-level holders: Gomez=7+5+5=17; Hill=5+3+3+3 preference points=14; Jones=5+5+5=15; Ikeda=3+3+3=9. Dube has current Level 4 and a three-interval limit; Gomez (17) is lower than Dube (18), and GS-12 is the least grade reduction, so offer Gomez’s GS-12. Hill, Jones, and Ikeda are also lower-standing but are at greater grade reductions; GS-9 Ikeda is four intervals below and outside Dube’s limit. Estrada has a current Level 5 rating and a three-interval limit. Gomez is higher-standing; Hill (14) and Jones (15) are lower-standing; offer Hill’s GS-11 as the least reduction. Ikeda is four intervals below and out of range. Brandt has current Level 2 and the 30%-disabled preference-eligible five-interval limit. Gomez, Hill, and Jones have higher standing than Brandt; Ikeda (9) is lower-standing and GS-9 is four intervals below, within Brandt’s extended limit. Offer Ikeda’s GS-9.
(d) If all offers are accepted, Dube, Estrada, and Brandt remain employed in the lower positions. Gomez, Hill, and Ikeda are displaced from the positions they alone are qualified to hold and have no stated other qualified position; they are the three employees separated from the agency. Quinn, Farouk, Alvarez, Chen, and Jones remain in their positions.
Q12.basis: 2026-15665, §§351.202(d)(2)(ii), 351.502(a), 351.503(a), (c), (f)(2)–(3), 351.504(a), 351.501(c), 91 FR 49218–49223; restoration protection and pass-over, §351.606(a), 91 FR 49223–49224 and preamble 91 FR 49203; assignment rights, §§351.701–.702, 91 FR 49225–49226. The preamble states the USERRA 180-day/one-year thresholds at 91 FR 49203.
Q12.uncertainty: The rule’s mandatory USERRA exception concerns the protection period remaining as of notice receipt. The stated 14-month absence establishes the one-year category under the preamble; the agency must document the expiration date and ordinary standing.

Q13.answer:
I find these checked preamble/text mismatches:

1. **Standing trigger—issued versus received.** The preamble says that standing is frozen on the date the RIF notice “is issued” (91 FR 49185). The regulatory text says standing is determined on the date the employee “receives a specific reduction in force notice” (§351.507(a)–(b), 91 FR 49223). A later passage correctly says “receives” (91 FR 49179, Executive Summary item 16; also 91 FR 49202, §351.805 discussion).
2. **Five-year assessment exception.** The Executive Summary describes the assessment exemption as applying if the employee held the same/similar position “within five years of the RIF” (91 FR 49179, item 13). The text specifies a five-year period **ending on the date the employee receives** the specific RIF notice (§351.702(a)(4)(v), 91 FR 49226). The section-by-section discussion states the notice-receipt endpoint correctly (91 FR 49205, §351.702 discussion).

I do not count a preamble omission of a regulatory detail as a mismatch, and I do not find a separate confirmed contradiction in the other section summaries checked.
Q13.uncertainty: The preamble’s phrase “within five years of the RIF” is imprecise; the operative text supplies the exact five-year endpoint.

Q14.answer:
(i) **Preamble/text differences in OPM’s appeals rule.** First, the preamble says §351.901(c) makes the procedures in “part 351” the sole and exclusive means of appeal (2026-15666, 91 FR 49244). As corrected, §351.901(c)(1) says the procedures in “this subpart” are the exclusive means (2026-17338, 91 FR 54796 correcting 2026-15666, 91 FR 49263). Second, the section analysis says the appellant must prove that the appeal was timely “and in the required form” (2026-15666, 91 FR 49248); §351.901(b)(1) lists timeliness, but not a separate burden element of proper form, while §351.903(a) separately states the appeal’s form/content requirements (91 FR 49263–49264). Third, the preamble summary says public posting is limited to protect “protected personnel information” (91 FR 49231); the correction changes the regulatory phrase to “protected personal information” (§351.909(f), 2026-17338, 91 FR 54796 correcting 2026-15666, 91 FR 49267).

(ii) **Proposal-to-final differences not acknowledged in the summary of changes.** (1) The final/corrected §351.901(c)(1) changes “this part” in the proposal to “this subpart”; the summary still describes the exclusive process as part 351 procedures. (2) §351.902(a) changes the filing object from reconsideration of an “initial appeal” under “this part” to reconsideration of an “initial decision” under “this subpart”; the summary does not identify that correction. (3) §351.901(c)(3) omits the Federal Labor Relations Authority from the proposed list of collateral forums, while the summary lists the final forums but does not call out the deletion. (4) §351.903(b) changes the agency-response deadline from “within 30 calendar days of the initial appeal” to “within 30 calendar days after service,” with a separate rule that the 30 days begin upon service; the summary does not mention that trigger clarification. (5) §351.905(c) removes the proposal’s authority to direct “any other appropriate action” and retains the more specific fact-development tools; the summary discusses narrowing audits/investigations but does not mention deleting that authority. (6) §351.906(b) changes mandatory sanctions (“OPM shall”) to discretionary sanctions (“OPM may”), and final §351.906(c) adds that sanctions must be proportionate, causally related, and no broader than necessary; the summary’s protective-order discussion does not identify either change.

(iii) The MSPB rule has conflicting transition statements. Its DATES text says it will not apply the rule to pending or newly filed cases concerning agency actions taken before the effective date of OPM’s rulemakings and will continue to hear those RIF appeals (2026-16456, 91 FR 51997). Its RIF preamble says MSPB will accept appeals where the agency issued the RIF notice before September 2 (91 FR 51997). But its later “Effective Date of Amendment” section says MSPB will adjudicate RIF appeals received after September 2 only where the RIF effective date preceded September 2 (91 FR 51998). OPM’s appeals rule, in turn, makes its process apply by **notice issuance** on or after September 2 (2026-15666, 91 FR 49230, DATES). Thus a pre-September 2 notice with a post-September 2 effective date is treated differently by the MSPB preamble and its later effective-date statement.
Q14.basis: OPM proposal: 2026-02576, 91 FR 5861–5877; OPM final rule: 2026-15666, 91 FR 49230–49267; OPM correction: 2026-17338, 91 FR 54796; MSPB final rule: 2026-16456, 91 FR 51997–51998. The corrections quoted above are part of the regulatory text as of November 14, 2026.
Q14.uncertainty: The MSPB transition inconsistency leaves the Board’s treatment of a pre-effective-date notice with a later effective separation unclear. The items in (i) are textual discrepancies, not conclusions about their legal effect.
